speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TABLING OF REPLY OF UNITED STATES
subtopic: GOVERNMENT CONCERNING RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the formal reply of the United States state department to our representations of March 8 concerning proposals that imports of oil from Canada and other sources should be restricted by legislation or by voluntary action. In view of the fact that our note was included in Hansard perhaps I should read this reply so that it could also appear there.
The reply is:
Reference is made to the Canadian embassy's aide-memoire of March 8,	1955, in which the
embassy set forth in some detail the views of the Canadian government with respect to certain legislation being considered in the United States which has the purpose of limiting the importation of petroleum.
The Department of State appreciates receiving this clear and comprehensive exposition of the Canadian viewpoint. The problems discussed in the aide-memoire are receiving very careful study and the security aspects, as well as the economic considerations, of trade in petroleum and petroleum products between the United States and Canada are being examined.
The Canadian government may rest assured that its views will be given the fullest and most sympathetic possible consideration. As the Canadian embassy is no doubt aware, the executive branch of the United States government has indicated to the congress that it is opposed to the amendment to H.R. 1 proposed by a number of senators which would have the effect of placing legislative limits on the importation of petroleum.
I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, and the house will appreciate that this reply is not very precise. This is not, I think, particularly surprising since the issues involved are currently being discussed actively both within the United States administration and in congress. The full significance of this brief communication from the state department can only, therefore, be determined after the outcome of these various discussions is known, and it is that outcome rather than this particular note which is important.
In the meantime, as I informed the house on Tuesday last, we have been assured by the state department orally that every effort is being made to give recognition to the factors which the Canadian government emphasized
in its earlier representations. While we cannot be certain about the final result I am hopeful that in the light of their own interest and of the considerations which we have brought to their notice, the United States government will deal with this question in a manner which will not interfere with the development of the trade in oil between Canada and the United States, which is of such importance to both countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TABLING OF REPLY OF UNITED STATES
subtopic: GOVERNMENT CONCERNING RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTATION
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members will welcome the information which has been given in regard to this very important subject. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has explained, there is some reservation in regard to the information given, for reasons Which we can all fully understand. I believe, however, it would be appropriate to point out that, having regard to the very close association between our two countries and to the extremely friendly relationship which has been regarded as an example, there are implications in one aspect of this matter which should be borne in mind.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce informed the house of the message which had been sent to the government of the United States at the time it was proposed that there be certain fixed limitations upon the movement of oil across our frontiers. It appears from the message that has gone from the state department to the appropriate committee of congress that every effort is being made by the government of the United States to prevent a rigid pattern of that type taking form. There was, however, one other aspect of this question which has not been dealt with as yet, and which I feel could have consequences which should not be ignored if there were not some satisfactory assurances in regard to it.
It will be recalled that there was a suggestion that, as an alternative to ordinary legislative procedure, there might be a method under which companies organized in the United States and transmitting oil to the United States might be called upon to produce by voluntary action the limitation which otherwise would be imposed by legislative provision.
Having regard to the very large investment of United States funds in Canada, and having

Questions
regard to the desirability of mutual confidence not only from the financial point of view but from every other point of view, I would hope that any attempt to use the power that might be exercised by the fact that the money control was in the United States would be given very careful consideration. It could undoubtedly lead to loss of confidence on the part of investors in the United States in some types of investments here. At the same time it could raise questions in this country as to the freedom of investments which we have always regarded as being vitally important, whether they came from there, from the United Kingdom or from any other country.
I mention this because this subject was regarded as of sufficient importance by the government to be brought forward in considerable detail; and in seeking information it was not only in the hope that any legislative restriction might be prevented but also in the hope that any indirect restriction might be avoided which could interfere with that very friendly relationship in financial affairs which has been so helpful to both countries.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: STUDY OF RADIOACTIVITY RESULTS, UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
1.	Is the Canadian government giving consideration to taking the initiative in urging the United Nations to make a study as to the extent to which atomic and hydrogen bomb tests can be made without grave danger to the human race, as requested by the federation of American scientists?
2.	If so, when will such action be taken?
3.	If not, what are the reasons for the government's decision?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STUDY OF RADIOACTIVITY RESULTS, UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
1.	No.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	The Canadian government has been in touch with friendly governments who, through the possession of atomic and thermonuclear weapons, have a direct interest in

this matter. Statements made recently by responsible officials of these governments indicate that tests so far have produced a general level of radioactivity which is remote from endangering human life.
Of course these matters should be kept, and are being kept, under constant study as indicated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the house on April 4. In addition to the investigations referred to by the minister at that time, the scientific conference on the peaceful uses of atomic energy to be held in Geneva in August will consider a number of problems related to the health and safety aspects of atomic energy, including biological and genetic effects and radiation injury and protection.
The government would be prepared to support any serious studies, which gave promise of increasing our knowledge of the problem. It is the view of the government, however, that it would serve no useful purpose for it to take any special initiative at this time of the kind referred to in the question. The government will continue to consult with friendly governments on this important matter.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for having given notice of his question. In some of the T-33 crashes the pilots were able to report by radio that they -were encountering difficulty. Whether or not radio communication is possible in such

circumstances depends of course upon distance, communications conditions and the rapidity with which an emergency may develop.

With respect to the 19 T-33 crashes which occurred in training command during the calendar year 1954, radio reports of difficulty were made in the case of five crashes, and in three of these five crashes there were no fatalities. Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for having given notice of his question. The Canadian experiment in the development of a coal-fired gas turbine engine by Professor Mordell at McGill University has been under way for several years under the sponsorship of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
About a year ago the machine was started on a test run. After about 50 hours' run certain weaknesses developed. After consultation among all the scientists connected with the project, it was decided that certain modifications were desirable before the tests were carried any further. When a test run of several hundred hours has been completed the results will then be made available to private industry. Any application of the machine to locomotive or other uses will then be up to private industry. We have reason to believe that the Mordell experiment is equal to or in advance of similar experiments in other countries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 19, as recorded at page 2971 of Hansard, I said I proposed to outline in some detail how Stalin of Russia and his friends conquered China, indicating the part played by Roosevelt at Yalta in destroying Chiang Kai-shek. On April 6 I made a few remarks indicating that same part played by Roosevelt.
On each of those dates, I had hoped to answer the statement made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) on March 24, 1955, concerning Chiang Kai-shek.

On April 6 I promised to read an excerpt from an editorial in a great United States newspaper, commenting upon the recent publication of the Yalta papers. The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) asked the name of the paper, and I promised to give it to him. I now give him the name of the paper and read the extract. The name of the paper is the New York Daily News, and it is dated March 18, 1955. It has a daily circulation of 2,050,000, which indicates that it is no third-rate or tenth-rate newspaper. The name of the editorial from which the extract comes is "The Sorry Record of Yalta." These are the words I culled from the editorial:
So Roosevelt sold Chiang Kai-shek down the river, with a lame excuse that he felt sure Chiang would agree afterward to virtually giving Russia Manchuria and the warm water port of Dairen. Thus, Roosevelt set the stage for the red conquest of China, the Korean war, and the present threat of communist conquest of all Asia.
And, I might add, of all the world.
I think that will indicate quite clearly that I am not alone in the position I take. The particular statement of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was this, as reported at page 2356 of Hansard:
How many Canadians or Americans understand why the Chinese people drove Chiang Kai-shek out of China?
Later on, as I recall, there were more remarks that indicated the reason he was driven out by the Chinese was that Chiang was "corrupt". In the same speech the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made three other statements which I shall not take time to read to the house at the present time, but the opening and closing words of which I shall give so they can be found readily by those who are interested. The first is on page 2358 of Hansard as follows:	"It is about
time ... continental United States." The next is: "He suggested... the United Nations." The next is: "I have told... peace in Asia."
Now, there is diametrical opposition between myself and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. This is wholly honest, and there is no political concern in the matter. He believes one thing; I believe another.
I think the issue between us must be decided by reference to authorities. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is a university graduate, I am sure. I am a university graduate. He has been principal of a high school for a good many years; so have I. Neither of us is accustomed to telling lies, and neither of us is much accustomed to getting things wrong. He has been in public life a good while; so have I. I shall now give the authorities which I propose to use and we
External Affairs
shall see which one of us can base his opinions on the sounder authority. In the time left to us in the present session I fancy the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and I shall have some entertainment.
These are the authorities to which I propose to refer. The first one is "China in Stalin's Grand Strategy." I have them all here on my desk so everybody can see them. It was written by Dr. Hu Shih, one-time ambassador to the United States during a period including 1939. The article is reprinted from Foreign Affairs, an American quarterly review, October 1950, copyrighted in 1950 by the Council on Foreign Relations, Incorporated. It was printed in the United States. I shall refer to this document whenever I have reason to refer to it by the words "Hu Shih". This will enable us to avoid repeating the name of this document so many times in Hansard, because with respect of every statement I make I am going to identify the document so there will be no question as to the soundness of what I shall state, or that the authorities to which I shall refer are valid.
The second document is "The Iron Curtain over America" which was written by Dr. John Beaty. It was first printed in 1951, and the eighth printing was in June, 1952. Dr. John Beaty is an M.A. of the University of Virginia, a Ph.D. of Columbia University, and a postgraduate of University of Montpellier in France. In 1941 he was called to active duty in the military intelligence service of the United States war department general staff, where he spent five years. In 1943 he was promoted to lieutenant colonel and made chief of the interview section. From 1946 to 1951 he devoted his time to intensive study preparing to write, and writing, "The Iron Curtain over America". Whenever I refer to this document I have just mentioned I shall do so by using the word "Beaty", which indicates the author.
I may say in addition, concerning this man whose works we are considering, that in 1942 he became a major and chief of the historical section in the intelligence department. He was one of the two editors of the daily secret "G2" reports issued to key persons in high places in the United States administration, giving the world picture as it had been four hours earlier. If a man like that does not get to know his way around the world, and what things are all about, I am sure it will be amazing to every hon. member of this house.
The third document to which I propose to refer is "The China Story" by Freda Utley, who is quoted as an authority by Dr. Beaty. I shall refer to "The China Story", 1951, by the use of the word "Utley". Freda Utley is

External Affairs
speaking from firsthand knowledge. She was in China in 1946-page 60 of Utley. She heard General Wedemeyer in Shanghai-Utley, 61. She spent six years in Russia-Utley, 63 and 108. She was in Chungking and Shanghai in 1946-Utley, page 71. She knew Li Tsung-jen well in Hankow in 1938 and talked with him again in 1946-Utley, page 83. She was correspondent for the London News-Chronicle in the summer and fall of 1938 and was in Hankow-Utley, 103.
She was personally acquainted with some of the leading figures of the minority who corrupted United States foreign policy in the Far East-Utley, 103. She knew Stilwell in Hankow-Utley, 105. She was herself for some time deceived by Chinese communists and revealed it in her book "China at War", 1939-Utley, page 265. She was very frank. She knew John P. Davies-Utley, 115. She spent eight days in Yenan in 1946-Utley, page 140. She knew Edgar Snow who wrote "Red Star over China"-Utley, page 140.
Besides this she draws most profusely and specifically from authorities of unchallengeable authenticity, such as original documents. For example, on page 30 of "The China Story" she says:
No one who takes the trouble to study the records can accept Acheson's statement.
That statement of Utley's pretty well applies to Acheson all the way across the board. She verifies this assertion by reference to Acheson's "Letter of Transmittal", to the white paper on "United States Relations with China, 1949" in her notes on page 263 of her book "The China Story". There seems to be very little doubt about the validity of Freda Utley.
The next document is "The Yalta Betrayal" published in 1953 by Felix Wittmer, a man who quotes original documents and lets them speak for themselves; a man whom Dr. Beaty occasionally cites as an authority, which alone pretty well qualifies him as being. worth listening to. The next is "Freedom's Case Agayrst Dean Acheson" by Felix Wittmer, a reprint from the American Mercury of April 1, 1952. 1 have that here, and I hold it up so all hon. members can see it. I shall refer to the pages of the reprint when I have occasion to refer to the article "Freedom's Case Against Dean Acheson".
In addition to these five documents I shall refer to certain smaller documents such as the McCarran committee hearings and other authentic publications. In every case the evidence to which I shall refer was taken under oath in a committee of one of the most solemn organizations in the world, the United States Senate. Finally there is the book "While You Slept" published in 1951

by John T. Flynn, who quotes abundantly and minutely from original documents.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I have endeavoured to be frank and straightforward with hon. members of the house. This is too serious a time in the world's history to be playing politics with a matter as serious as Formosa or China or Chiang Kai-shek. It is far too serious for any hon. member of this house to get up and make pronouncements on any of these three things without knowing exactly what he is talking about, and without considering everything he says. It is true that there will be honest disagreement, and I am going to explain that in a minute. I have done my utmost to play square with the house and the country and I welcome honest criticism, but I hope there will be no silly, superficial political criticism, because this is too serious a time for politics. I can play politics if I want to, but I prefer not to do it. We are too much under the shadow of disaster for anything of that sort.
Let me assure my C.C.F. friends that there is nothing political in my position today, as I said in my opening remarks, nor in anything I say. We are living in exceedingly dangerous days when the Christian religion, in fact all religion based upon a belief in God, is in extreme peril. Back in June, 1945, there was published in the Reader's Digest for June an article under the caption "The Fate of the World is at Stake in China". In referring to that article Freda Utley says that only a very few publications in the United States dared to print an article with a heading like that. In other words there was already in the United States a censorship which rendered it next to impossible for any newspaper to publish the truth about China. That serves to show how desperate is the condition we have fallen into up to the present time. It is true today, truer than it was in 1945, that the fate of the world is at stake in China. I think it can safely be said that it is at stake in Formosa.
I shall ask the minister later on to tell us why he feels so sure about what he has referred to as neutralizing Formosa. I think we shall give him an opportunity some time to explain that to us; but meanwhile under the circumstances, I am inclined to think that neutralizing Formosa is a desperately serious proposal.
Let me ask my C.C.F. friends whether or not they might not have been reading the wrong books or the wrong kind of books and periodicals. In saying that I am not being mean or political. I think everybody realizes that I have been open and aboveboard and

fair up to the present time, and I intend so to continue. I expect those who are in the house to be just exactly that way.
Let me point out some things which astounded me when I learned them within the last few months.
In the United States, "the communist party line, beginning on October 2, 1942, was anti-Chiang Kai-shek". This is verified in "Freedom's Case Against Dean Acheson", as stated on page 9 of the American Mercury reprint-and it is an accurate document. When it is quoted by a man such as Dr. John Beaty, an ordinary person like you and me had better hold his peace until he is sure he knows whereof he speaks.
Again, Lawrence Salisbury in 1943 resigned from the United States state department to become editor of the Institute of Pacific Relations' fortnightly publication, Far Eastern Survey, and in this capacity he inaugurated a virulent anti-Chinese nationalist and proChinese communist campaign paralleling that of the communist Daily Worker, the Nation and the New Republic-Utley, page 150.
I think some people will be astonished to learn that the Nation and the New Republic are communist publications.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: We are.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If you are in any doubt about it just look yourself at Utley, page 150. That is how serious the situation is.
Mr. Philip Jessup, as director of the Institute of Pacific Relations, started in 1943 a virulent smear campaign against nationalist China much like the one conducted against Premier William Aberhart of Alberta. I had occasion to tell you about this the night before last. There never grew up in the Dominion of Canada a more straightforward man or a man more honestly interested in reform than Premier Aberhart; yet that man was lied about all over the world and particularly all over the American continent. I suppose that most ladies would have drawn aside their skirts if they knew they were coming into the same room where he was; he was a man fighting the whole power of the synagogue of Satan, whatever that may be. I shall drop the word "synagogue" and say "the hosts of Satan".
The people who are seeking to destroy Christianity and religion, Chou En-lai and all the people who believe in the rulers of Russia, belong to that fellowship, and they do not mean maybe. What they mean is that the Christian religion has to be destroyed, and that they will destroy it as surely as they are allowed to get power. You cannot say that the people who represent that kind of thing
External Affairs
are emanating from Christianity. The people who opposed Aberhart are the same kind of people as those opposing Chiang Kai-shek now. The facts about Jessup appear in Utley, page 152.
May I now review Chiang's history in bare outline since 1912, and in the light of that history call upon men to use their plain common sense? There are men who say that Chiang was corrupt. I would like to see any member of this house undertake the job which Chiang Kai-shek did from 1926 on and avoid corruption in a huge country such as China, with very few trained and able people to help him. He was after all only a military general, not a statesman; not a dictator, just the president of a republic. I know that all sounds strange, but it is true, and the truth does sound strange after communist lies have done with it.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What about the Christian Science Monitor?

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I shall deal with the Christian Science Monitor in good time, but I wish to give the general facts. China is an enormous country with many different kinds of people and many different languages. It is a very poor country. It is a primary producing country; it has very few factories, and it has poor communications in every way and poor local organizations. It has 450 million people. The very idea of one man even attempting to govern a mass like that is enough to repel a person. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has been a school principal. You can imagine what kind of difficulty he would have if he had a school of 450 million pupils and did not have trained teachers to help him but had assistants who knew no more than the children themselves. That is the first thing.
Let us remember that the Manchu dynasty, as a result of the Manchu conquest, had been in power in China for more than 200 years. Thus there were Manchu war lords over the districts in China, much as we had the lords over the feudal districts in Britain, only not nearly as intelligent as the British lords.
Sun Yat-sen in 1911-1912 established the first republic in Asia. Let us remember then that China was a republic and realize that the man in charge of a republic does largely what his assistants want him to do as well as what he wants to do himself. Chiang Kai-shek was made president of the Whampoa military academy. His job was to train military leaders who could help Sun Yat-sen conquer the Manchu war lords.
Sun Yat-sen died in 1925. Chiang Kai-shek as I have said was merely a military

External Affairs
leader; that was all he pretended to be. Being the kind of military leader he was, it took all his time to learn war. He was trained in Moscow and Japan; he got all the training he could get so as to become a successful military leader. He is one of the most skilful military leaders on earth today. He proved that conclusively in an incident about which I shall be telling you in a moment.
In 1925-26 he had to take over the leadership in China though almost entirely without knowledge or experience in political government. He was general of the army, yet he was called upon to take over Sun Yat-sen's responsibilities to govern. He established the national government with the advice of his elders on April 18, 1927. In the very year in which Chiang set up this national republic, Stalin established the Chinese communist party. Stalin established the communist red army also in the same year. Chiang Kai-shek had had to go north in 1926 to conquer most of China, to depose those Manchu war lords or bring them under control. He had singular success in this effort, and did simply marvellous things.
He had been in charge of China for only six years, and during that time he had been faced with most dreadful difficulties when in 1931 the Japanese attacked in Manchuria. It was in the far north, and it was very difficult for him to meet them. He had exceedingly trying difficulties then. He had to show extremely wise statesmanship. The Japanese were anxious to engage him in a full-scale war, when he was in no way prepared for such a war but they were. He had to fight a delaying action to hold them back as far as he could to prevent getting into a full-scale war in which he would have been annihilated.
This he did. He allowed them to take Manchuria and they established the puppet state of Manchukuo. as they called it. He then had a short time of six more years before the Japanese attacked on a full scale in 1937. One pathetic thing about the war that ensued was that the Japanese were plentifully supplied by the British and Americans with all the latest kinds of instruments of war, while Chiang Kai-shek had to fight with very meagre weapons. He was fighting the Japanese in 1937, and he continued to fight Japanese from 1937 to 1945.
Now I ask the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar if he thinks he could bring in reforms in a country like China and fight at the same time an army of 1,500,000 Japanese, as Chiang had to do, and, at the same time, look after a Russian communist organization in China

and a Russian communist Chinese army. Think of the difficulty in raising the money to equip an army such as Chiang required! This is what Chiang Kai-shek did.
I spoke about 1,500,000 Japanese soldiers. All during the war, from the time we got into it in 1941, he was holding that 1,500,000 Japanese pinned against the east Chinese coast. If they could have gone abroad or could have gone to Australia and New Zealand, I ask hon. members what might have happened to us and what might have happened to the United States. Let us bear that in mind when we remember the absolutely terrible things the United States has done to Chiang.
Over much of this time he fought the communists as well as the Japanese. There was a time during which the communists co-operated with him, but there were times when they turned their armies against him, made a flank attack against him and did him serious harm, and then blamed him for mismanagement. The story is something terrible to read about, but it is all given in Hu Shih's "China in Stalin's Grand Strategy" and Hu Shih cites men who are recognized as world authorities, such as David J. Dallin.
There is no question about the truth of what I am saying. At one time while he was fighting the Japanese Chaing had to leave some of his assistants to rule China and hold the Japanese while he set out on a 6,000 mile march driving the communist army up into the north, destroying 60,000 of its best men and getting things into position so that he had a ghost of a chance to fight the Japanese. How do you suppose he could have instituted reforms during these periods?
Throughout all his rule he struggled against foreign interests. One of the things that caused Sun Yat-sen to rise was the fact that the British had in China their sphere of influence, as a result of which they had managed to get the Chinese to sign agreements which were greatly disadvantageous to the Chinese; and various other nations had similar spheres of influence in China. The result of that imperialistic control was that it was next to impossible to govern China well at all. Throughout the time he was doing what I have been talking about, namely fighting the Russian communist organization, the Russian communist armies and the Japanese armies, he had to be steadily displacing these outside interests so he would have a chance to govern China.
He constantly struggled against poverty, ignorance and vast numbers in China. Just think that matter over. There were 450 million people spread over such a wide area as that of China. At the same time-and it is

a thing which must not be forgotten-he had a paucity of generals and a paucity of administrators. To hear some people talk, and to read some of the nonsense they write, you would imagine that skilful administrators simply sprang up out of the desert and that skilful generals merely rained down out of the sky. Where do you suppose he obtained enough capable men? How do you suppose he could govern a country of 450 million people without skilful administrators? How do you suppose he could hold out in China without skilful military leaders? He had to take what he could get.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to what happened in Formosa. I suppose Chiang Kai-shek sent the best man he had, but that man was a military leader; he was not supposed to be a governor. He probably made bad mistakes. No doubt he did. But with all the other 450 million to take care of, and the vast hordes of red China coming down against him, how possibly could Chiang Kai-shek personally supervise Formosa to see that everything was done right? Just put yourselves in that position. Just do a little bit of realistic thinking.
He was constantly being stalked by Stalin. According to this document by Hu Shih I have read from, Stalin started back in 1924, and he stalked Chiang Kai-shek constantly for 25 years, because he knew if he got control of China, he would have a chance of controlling the world. Just as Lenin said, so thought Stalin; whoever controls China will control the world.
What was the result of all this effort? Chiang came through to 1945 triumphantly. There will be some who will doubt that, but it is given right here in Hu Shih. Maybe I shall get to the reading of the passage. He came through to 1945 triumphantly.
Even after all the United States and Russia were able to do to destroy him, Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Formosa in 1949 with dignity and with constancy, facing the foe with faith and determination and confidence.
What are the facts about what he left behind him? Some would think he was a victim of a disgraceful rout. Read "The Iron Curtain over America" and you will find that such thinking is entirely erroneous. What did he leave behind? He left behind on the mainland 1,250,000 Chinese soldiers-Beaty, page 146-who were ready to give their lives for Chiang Kai-shek. Do you suppose he accomplished that by being corrupt? According to Major General Claire Chennault he left behind him 150 million ardently loyal people all along the south and west China borders, almost as many people as there were people in the United States-all ready to give their
External Affairs
lives for Chiang Kai-shek. He had with him on Formosa 200 to 250 planes. He had an effective navy. He had 600,000 loyal soldiers -see Beaty, 146

who retreated to Formosa with him. He was so strong and potentially effective that it required the Korean war- and this is a new slant on the Korean war, and it is one that turns one sick, but I am going to put the evidence before you-and the United States seventh fleet thrown in front of him to keep him from regaining China.
I am going to put the evidence before you to show that apparently the Korean war was deliberately engineered by people in the United States in order to enable the United States seventh fleet to be put between Chiang Kai-shek and red China so as to keep Chiang Kai-shek from recapturing China.

That is right. How could he permit himself to be deluded into thinking that the Chinese people threw Chiang Kai-shek out of China? What would plain common sense tell you in the face of all this? I shall have to take up the matter of what actually caused the trouble at a later time. I have not the time to do so now. But let me recall again that Roosevelt at Yalta on February 11, 1945, gave Russia "pre-eminent interests" in Manchuria and in north China as a result of which unless Chiang Kai-shek could perform miracles Russia would be able

External Affairs
to conquer China. I referred to that matter the other day. Maybe I shall have time to look into it at a later time.
May I now refer to a few instances in Chiang's life-and just a few. I will talk as long as I can and then I shall have to finish this at a later time.
Here is the first instance: In November, 1943, at the Cairo conference as reported in the statement of December 1-and you will find it in "The Yalta Betrayal" at pages 109 and 110-it was declared by Roosevelt that "all the territories Japan has stolen from the Chinese, such as Manchuria, Formosa and the Pescadores, shall be restored to the republic of China". That was in 1943. Did Roosevelt not know what he was doing? I do not know why he did the horrible thing he did two years later, but that is what he committed himself to in 1943. The evidence is here in "The Yalta Betrayal" at pages 109 and 110, if hon. members wish to read it for themselves.
Here is the second instance: In February, 1945, at Yalta, Roosevelt agreed to let Russia acquire what was to be in effect a permanent position of power in China by granting Russia -and I am quoting Freda Utley at page 3, although I am not putting her words in quotation marks-
1.	The "lease" of Port Arthur to Russia as a naval base;
2.	The "internationalization" of Dairen with "pre-eminent rights" for the Soviet union in this largest of China's northeastern ports;
3.	The "joint operation" of the Manchurian railways by China and Russia, with the "preeminent interests" of the Soviet union safeguarded.
See "The China Story", page 3.
Hon. members do not need to be told what that meant. It meant that Russia could walk in and take over everything, which she did. Pre-eminent rights! This meant the two, China and Russia, would be working together, with Russia having pre-eminent rights. You might as well harness a lamb and a lion together and expect the lamb to have a fair chance.
In the Yalta agreement in 1945 Roosevelt sowed the wind from which Chiang Kai-shek within five years, beggared by abundant additional United States treachery, was to reap, and be almost wrecked by, the whirlwind; and before which in 1955, only 10 years later, the whole anti-communist world cowers in imminent danger of being utterly devastated by the tornado.
Here is the third incident. In July, 1945, Truman confirmed the Yalta agreement at [Mr. Blackmore.l
Potsdam against the earnest advice of 50 high-ranking United States officers whose report to General Marshall accurately analysed the situation as it affected China, and forecast exactly what would happen. They made it quite clear that we did not need Russia in the war. Japan was already beaten, and to let Russia come into that war would be a calamity of the first magnitude. Yet in the face of all this Truman confirmed these Yalta agreements. See the Russell committee hearings, part IV, June 21, 1951, page 2916.
Here is the fourth incident. In November 1946, as the white paper on China states:
The-Chinese nationalist-government's forces had occupied most of the areas covered by its demands to the Chinese communists in June and during later negotiations and had reached what turned out to be the highest point of its military position after V-J day.
Does this indicate in Chiang a man who is inept, a man who is corrupt, a man who is ineffective? Or does it indicate a man who towers above men in his character and ability? See Utley, page 16. All this in spite of Roosevelt, Truman, and General Marshall! I want to talk about General Marshall and what he did, by and by, and tell the outrageous things he did to Chiang Kai-shek in 1946.
This is the fifth incident. In September, 1947-remember now, after all the bad things that had been done in 1946-General Albert Wedemeyer, in his survey submitted to the United States president, said the-
-Chiang government had large forces still under arms and was in control of all China south of the Yangtze river, much of north China, with some footholds in Manchuria.
This is a quotation from Beaty's "The Iron Curtain over America", page 118. This again in spite of the further abominations committed against Chiang by Marshall and Truman in 1946! I shall elaborate on those at a later time.
Here is the sixth incident: On July 17, 1949, Owen S. Lattimore, in an article in the Sunday Compass entitled "South Korea- Another China", pointed out that for the United States state department in relation to China, "The problem was how to allow them-China-to fall without making it look as if the United States had pushed them." There is no further word necessary.

speechtext:
should like to make some observations about the Far East, Mr. Speaker. I shall simply say of Europe that, although the situation is fraught with danger, it is by no means fraught with disaster. I am not so cheerful about the Far East, however. I believe that most Canadians are alarmed about the inconsistencies and what seems at times the belligerency of United States foreign policy in Asia. I feel that the time has come for some plain speaking.
I believe it was Secretary of State Dulles who said that Canada is no satellite of the United States, and I feel we should make that fact abundantly clear. It is clear that the explosive situation in the Far East results from the clash of interests between the United States and communist China, and also from the chief satellite of the United States in that area, nationalist China. As a fundamental premise we can readily divest ourselves of the pernicious influence of the communist propaganda gramophone theme that the United States is a world aggressor intent upon thrusting the American way of life down the throats of others. One cannot live in Canada and believe that the United States people are imperialists. But one can believe they can be misguided, albeit they are perfectly sincere. This is the nub of my submissions today.
It will be recalled immediately how important the Marshall plan was in the rehabilitation of Europe. This was a magnanimous and generous stroke which I believe mirrored the feelings of individual United States citizens. We all believe in the objective of world peace, but this does not imply that we agree on the means by which it may be achieved. As Milton said, one has the right to think, to utter and to argue according to one's conscience, and it is that opportunity I am availing myself of today.
Toward the end of 1954 most Canadians felt that progress was being made in working out a modus operandi with the communist world. It appeared that President Eisenhower had taken over active command of the United States foreign policy. The majority decision of the joint chiefs of staff to participate in the defence of Dien Bien Phu and in the prospective defence of Quemoy were both vetoed by the President. Some attributed his
External Affairs change of attitude to the visit of Sir Winston Churchill to Washington in June; others thought it was because of his realization of the awful consequences of the H-bomb, and still others thought it was the result of the enthusiastic reception he received on the hustings during the congressional election, when he talked about a world at peace. Whatever the reason, it was gratifying to hear less blustering from the state department, particularly in reference to the Far East, and to hear more emphasis on the constructive working out of a modus vivendi with the communist world. It was widely felt here that the President was firmly exercising his presidential prerogative in foreign affairs and was a better judge than his advisers on the great questions of war and peace, and that he truly reflected the feelings of that great nation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are confused again. We thought Chiang Kai-shek was to be restrained, and now we fear he may be unleashed. Pronouncements from the state department have again become turgid and equivocal. Is the seventh fleet now to defend Quemoy and Matsu, which Sir Anthony Eden recently asserted were indubitably Chinese?
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on Quemoy and Matsu. It was both gratifying and reassuring to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs state that any eruption there would not be our war. Mr. Speaker, we have no business at all intervening in a civil war struggle over those islands. Hon. members know that the question of whether or not the United States would fight over those islands rests with the President, and I agree that Mr. Eisenhower is a humble and sincere man dedicated to peace. But the basis upon which he is to make a decision, I understand, is whether or not he believes that the Chinese communists will use Quemoy and Matsu as a springboard for an invasion of Formosa. Therefore at best the President's opinion will be only a guess, and the peace of the world, I submit, is too important to hinge upon the guess of even such a good man as the President.
In February it will be recalled that congress gave the President carte blanche to defend Formosa and "such related positions" as he deemed necessary. Then came the revelation that Britain and Canada would not support such a policy, particularly as this position seemed to involve Quemoy and Matsu. The ground-swell of public opinion in the United States against the ndministration's ambiguous policy slowly grew into a perceptible roar.
In the April 3 edition of the New York Times, Governor Harriman of New York was

External Affairs
quoted as saying that the administration's policy disregarded "the sensibilities of either our Asian or European friends and allies", and then he went on to say, "It has not only been illogical but deadly dangerous to arrogate to ourselves"-meaning the United States-"the sole responsibility for decisions which involve the future of many peoples."
Senator Spessard Holland, a conservative Florida Democrat, issued a statement indicating only public resistance in his state to going to war over Quemoy and Matsu. Mr. James Reston, Washington correspondent of the New York Times, pointed out in the issue of April 3 that to argue that the defence of the offshore islands is necessary to the defence of Formosa is almost like arguing that the loss of Staten island, a ferryboat ride from Manhattan, would jeopardize the defence of Bermuda. He went on to state that this argument is made against the testimony by the joint chiefs of staff, and that they can defend Formosa even if Quemoy and Matsu are taken.
As a result of all these audible rumblings of dissent the administration began discussions with Britain, Canada and other allies on the possibility of a joint guarantee for the defence of Formosa. Conceivably this could be a face-saving substitute for the original demand for a cease-fire as the price for yielding Quemoy and Matsu.
Then Mr. Adlai Stevenson, in an important and significant foreign policy address, urged the administration to consult with its friends and allies, and even the uncommitted Asian states, asking them to join with the United States in an open declaration condemning the use of force in the Korean straits and to agree to stand with the United States in the defence of Formosa. Alternatively he suggested that the United States submit a resolution to the United Nations general assembly to condemn any effort to alter the present status of Formosa by force. It is interesting to note that the day after Mr. Stevenson made the speech, Secretary of State Dulles in effect endorsed Mr. Stevenson's speech, and it would appear that Mr. Stevenson had smoked out a clarification of the administration's position.
I would think that Mr. Stevenson's first proposition woud be unacceptable to the noncommitted Asian states, and indeed to ourselves and to Britain as well.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has repeatedly stated in this house that our foreign policy in the Far East will be in consonance with the principles of the United Nations and with decisions made by that organization in the Far East. But a general assembly resolution would have, I should

think, a good chance of success and, of equal importance, it would remove the terrifying responsibility for this decision from the shoulders of President Eisenhower and turn it over to the United Nations, where it belongs. I would humbly urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as a distinguished world statesman, to use his good offices toward this end, and if need be to take the initiative in bringing this before the United Nations assembly.
May I now consider those countries in the Far East where the yeast of revolution has been most ceaselessly fermenting. Countries such as India, Pakistan and Ceylon have now achieved independent status within the commonwealth. Indonesia, Burma, Indochina and the Philippines have achieved self-determination. Siam alone seems to be wallowing in the past. Japan is rapidly recovering from the ravages of war and defeat. But the key country in Asia is China, which has undergone a successful revolution, and a complete one too.
Briefly the fundamental raison d'etre of the Asian revolution is that it is a struggle for self-determination against the colonialism which reached its peak in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The people of the Far East are impressed more with the positive materialistic achievements of Russian communism than depressed with the ruthless and abhorrent extirpation of the freedom and dignity of the individual. They want food; they want to be treated like human beings. As Mr. Adlai Stevenson put it so succinctly, "They want rice and respect".
As for the Chinese people's government, there seems to be incontrovertible evidence that they are the effective government of over 500 millions of Chinese. At Geneva they were recognized as such, as the de facto government. Most of the important Asian countries as well as the United Kingdom and the Scandinavian governments, among others, recognize the People's Republic of China as the de jure government as well.
In spite of the brusqueness and even rudeness which characterizes their dealings with the west, in spite of their truculence and obstruction, they are governing China, moving into a hiatus created in great part by the misgovernment of Chiang Kai-shek and the Kuomintang so that in effect it was not difficult for the communists to take over.
That Chiang, the successor to the redoubtable Sun Yat-sen, should fritter away the basis of a Chinese democratic state and lose the democratic revolution by misrule is, I submit, one of the tragedies of our times. So I say we should consider recognizing the government of the People's Republic of

China, but make it contingent upon a general settlement in the Far East, particularly concerning the question of Formosa, through the United Nations.
It is simply a matter of facing facts. It is trite to say, but should be reiterated, that recognition does not mean approval. We certainly do not approve of the totalitarian policies of the Soviet union, but we recognize her existence and her government. I believe Mr. Churchill put it most neatly. In stating the difference between recognition and approval he said, "Mr. Speaker, I recognize the member for Ebbw Vale", who is, of course, Mr. Aneurin Bevan, "but I don't like him."
Second, we can never expect China to enter into a modus operandi with the west if we fail to make the fundamental overture of diplomatic recognition. It should never be forgotten that the Chinese revolution was primarily an indigenous one. The men of the long march were certainly not Russian satellites, as Professor Dennis Brogan has said. But our present policy of treating them as pariahs in the human society serves only to throw them more and more tightly into the willing arms of the Russian bear.
This policy I advocate seems to me to be plain common sense. I am not advocating a neutralist policy for this country. I aver unreservedly that our star is firmly placed in the western firmament; but in Asia I am much more willing to listen to Prime Minister Nehru, who is an Asian, a fellow member of our great commonwealth, and a firm democrat, than to the tergiversations of the state department and the bellicose vacuity of the so-called China lobby.
I concur in the reasoning that Formosa should be placed under the aegis of the United Nations for the time being. It is true that in the 1890's Formosa was ceded to China and then subsequently recaptured by the Japanese, but I submit it is only fundamental justice to see how the Formosans feel about it. After all they are not Chinese, nor are they Japanese. It would seem to me that this would be a good spot to apply the principle of self-determination. But by no means let us be drawn into a shooting war over Formosa. I would say that the quickest way for the west to alienate the numberless masses of Asia is to start dropping bombs on China. Of course, if a world war should erupt our position is irrevocable.
Let us, therefore, strive to use our good offices to effect an equitable and just solution in the Far East. Let us make every effort to avoid a world holocaust which in Sean O'-50433-192
External Affairs
Casey's phrase would make us "step over time into eternity". My respectful submission is that the means I have just outlined are essential and imperative to that end.

Mr. Speaker, this morning's newspapers told us that the Chinese communists were engaged in intense military preparations and that the United States had sent their chief of staff and their under secretary of defence to Formosa to inquire into the situation on the spot.
It is quite evident that there remains an imminent danger of war in the China sea and the Chinese question is the most serious of all those facing us at this time.
There seem to be many doubts here, in Canada, with regard to the position of our country in connection with this problem. The policy of this country, in spite of a great many speeches and statements from our minister, remains as vague as before. In any case, there is nothing new in that.
We need only remind ourselves that a year ago, approximately, on a tour around the world, our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated while in Asia, in the Philippines, to be exact, and in Korea, that sooner or later this country would have to recognize communist China. The Prime Minister made that statement at the time he was in Korea visiting our troops who had just fought against the army of this same communist China. The reaction, in the country, to statements of the Prime Minister was one of surprise especially since he took good care during the same trip not to land in Formosa and visit the Chiang Kai-sheks.
There must have been, also, an extraordinary reaction to those statements of the Prime Minister within the United States state department.
One must hope that the Prime Minister at that time wished to convey, in a somewhat naive way perhaps, that Canada would be ready to make every sacrifice to ensure peace to the world, that our country wished to be on good terms with every nation of the world even with communist nations and that we are a peaceful nation adverse to the waging of war against anyone. But today our government is moved by a vastly different purpose, and it goes to the other extreme. Where before it wanted to flirt with communist China, it is ready now to commit our country. And it lets the United States know that it would be unthinkable for us to remain neutral if they were engaged in a major war with that

External Affairs
same communist China that our own Prime Minister was ready to recognize just a little over a year ago.
Of course conditions have changed in the last twelve months. As a matter of fact the United States have decided to defend Formosa for Chiang Kai-shek and, what is more tragic, to defend the islands of Quemoy and Matsu.
The danger of war is extremely serious at this time in the China sea. The Chinese nationalists and the American military leaders claim that the islands of Matsu and Quemoy are necessary for the defence of Formosa. They wait only for the decision of the President of the United States to defend them and to keep them in the hands of the nationalists, even if those islands cannot be defended without invading the mainland or resorting to atomic bombing. And yet the disastrous effects of the Hiroshima bombing on the moral prestige of the Americans among Asiatic peoples is something that can never be measured.
Even England, faithful ally of the United States, refuses to become involved with our neighbours to the south, and does all she can to restrain them. Canada should follow this example and urge Washington to let these islands go, as they cannot be defended anyway. As far as Formosa is concerned, let us hold a referendum there under the guidance of the United Nations.
That would be better than to make speeches like the one delivered in Toronto by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), a speech which conveys the impression that this country was in a hurry to commit itself and that this government did not want to miss the opportunity to embark upon another international venture.
We have international obligations as a NATO member, and also as a member of the United Nations; but that is apparently not enough, because one of our ministers had to anticipate conclusions and make statements equivalent to this completely colonial slogan: "When the United States are at war, we are at war".
Obviously, our allies to the south are our closest allies, and any international problem which our allies have to face affects us. We must therefore give them all possible support inasmuch as they are the most powerful western state which has to assume tragic responsibilities and to lead a cold war against the Soviets and their puppet states.
But there is a difference between this and going as far as to tell the whole world that

every major war involving the United States will also involve us.
In 1914 and 1939 Canada was engaged in major wars in which our participation was meant to save the very existence of democracy in the world. Nevertheless, in the first world wide conflict our friends to the south waited until 1917 before they declared war. During the last war they waited until they were attacked at Pearl Harbor before taking up arms on our side.
Apparently, though, the government believes that this country must commit itself to any kind of adventure.

speechtext: On a point of order: Does the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) mean by that that the Secretary of State for External Affairs recently stated that when the United States are at war, Canada is necessarily at war also?

speechtext:
Formerly the saying was: "When England is at war, Canada is at war too". Nowadays, the old colonial motto is flourished under a different form: "When the United States are at war, Canada is at war".
What becomes of our independence with all that? The government seems to think little of it.

The minister may have spoken thus in order to obtain from the United States a more generous attitude toward us with respect to commerce.
Well, if that is the reason for his last speech in Toronto, you must admit that it has been a complete flop, as evidenced by the stand taken by the United States on the GATT agreements and, more recently, by the statement which was made on the oil issue by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), and the long silence of the American administration on that same issue. While the United States is reluctant to encourage the development of our oil resources which are essential for the defence of the whole western hemisphere, we are in a hurry to tell them that if they become involved in a major war we cannot but rush into that war at once.
It is obvious that the United States is essentially and vitally important for our trade. But it is unthinkable that our Secretary of State for External Affairs should commit our future and give up all thought of independence or neutrality in the event of a major war involving our neighbours to the south.
The policy of this government seems to be that Canada should take part in every venture and that her real independence can never be asserted.
Between recognizing communist China, an idea to which the Prime Minister was partial, and going to war against that country there is a middle road which it should be the goal of our Canadian diplomacy to follow. (Text):
