speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I object to the way in which this debate has been carried on. The organization of the debate has been bad. I see no reason for a debate being started about a month ago and carried on in this hit or miss fashion without any continuity whatsoever. But it has had one advantage, at least to myself. I was able to go home and talk with various groups of people about the declared policy of the minister, and to get the reaction of my own constituents, and have certain convictions of my own confirmed.
It is almost a truism to say that one of the affirmative purposes of foreign policy is to try to create such conditions that the people of Canada can live in peace and security. The negative aspect of foreign 50433-192J
External Affairs
policy is to try to avoid war. On both counts I do not find the policy of the government at all reassuring. We had from the minister an analysis of the situation in Asia with which I find myself in substantial agreement. I think what he said was right. We are engaged in a battle for men's minds. We have to win that battle. The minister knows how to go about it; but what the minister has said and what government policy is are two entirely different things without any reference whatsoever to each other.
The minister gave an analysis of Formosa, and my feeling was and still is that to some extent he was giving the Pentagon the green light to go ahead. But not even the Pentagon has gone quite as far in some ways as has one of the minister's colleagues. I suppose it must have been with some trepidation that the government learned that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was going to Australia. Possibly they were worrying about what he would say, what commitments he would make and what statements of policy he would enunciate which would provide some embarrassment for those left here.
The minister told us in his speech that we have engaged in no commitment to share in the defence of Formosa; he said that our obligations in this matter arise only out of our responsibility as a member of the United Nations. But apparently his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is not of the same mind, according to a press dispatch today, part of which is in direct quotation marks. It is again possible that this is another evidence of the occupational disease of ministers in being misquoted, as referred to by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron). However, as I say, some of this is in direct quotation marks. This dispatch is dated Canberra, Thursday, April 21, and is by the British United Press. The minister was attending a press conference and the report reads:
"Canada agreed with Australia's stand on the Formosa crisis," he said. "We take the same view as Prime Minister Menzies and are prepared to go full out for Formosa but I do not think we can go full out for the offshore islands of Quemoy and Matsu which historically are a part of China."
Here is a new enunciation of government policy. The second in command in the government says the government is prepared to go full out for Formosa. We ought to know, and know very soon, whether this is a new statement of policy on the part of the government or whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce is giving assurances to the Australians which I am convinced the people of Canada are not prepared to give.

External Affairs
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce is labouring under what I hope is a delusion and misapprehension, is it not conceivable also that our friends to the south may be labouring under the same delusion and misapprehension as to what is the real opinion of the people of Canada? When the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was speaking in this debate he told the minister that when speaking in the house he had watered down the remarks he had made in Toronto. I read the speech which the minister gave in Toronto, and I listened to and read his speech here. I probably have no knowledge whatsoever of semantics, but if there was any dilution it was not obvious to me.
I think the hon. member for Prince Albert was labouring under the same sort of delusion as certain newspapermen in Ottawa were labouring under after the visit of the United States secretary of state, Mr. Dulles. After Mr. Dulles had spoken I read in several newspapers that members of parliament were impressed. Perhaps that was the right word to use, but I am not quite sure in what context they used the word "impressed" because some of us were so impressed-that "some" extends beyond the members of my party-that we had some difficulty falling asleep that night just wondering what the secretary of state of the United States had in mind.
What the minister of external affairs said-and this is the important part-was that if the people of the United States were engaged in a major war in which their very existence as a people was at stake we could not stay out of it. The question arises as to who decides when the existence of the United States is at stake. Is it going to be the prerogative of this sovereign parliament to make that decision, or is it going to be decided for us outside the borders of this country? Perhaps that is a matter which only time will decide, but as far as we in the C.C.F. are concerned this parliament and this country are going to make the decision, and nobody else is going to do it for us.
We are faced with problems in Asia which we either solve or I think we may perish. The United States feels that communist aggression in Asia is a menace to its security. The United States feels that further aggression must be stopped. I cannot see how the offshore islands of Matsu and Quemoy, if they were occupied by communist China, would be a menace to the security of the people of Canada. As a matter of fact I cannot see how the occupation of Formosa by the same troops would be a menace to the people of Canada.

There are others who disagree with me. I am certainly not advocating the handing over of Formosa to Peking, but I fail to see, in terms of logistics or anything else, how the occupation of these offshore islands can possibly affect our security. But there are those in the United States, and some in high positions, who affirm that their security would be imperilled were the offshore islands to be lost.
The United States feel that the Chinese want to control southeast Asia, and I think they are quite right. Therefore the United States feel that they must persuade as many as possible of the people in southeast Asia to join them in a fight against communism. In that respect they are all wrong, because the people of southeast Asia are not remotely interested in this western fight against communism. They are most interested in the fight against poverty, and I think we can save them for our side if the policies as enunciated by the minister are carried out by the government.
On the other side of the medal, China feels that the presence of the nationalist government in Formosa is a constant threat to it. I happen to disagree. I do not think that Chiang Kai-shek and his troops present a menace at all to the mainland of China. Nevertheless I wonder how I would feel if I came from British Columbia and there was a potential enemy power on Vancouver island. I think I might feel as the Chinese do with a hostile government within 200 miles of their borders. The Chinese feel that Formosa is a threat as long as Chiang Kai-shek and his myrmidons are there; it is a threat which has to be eradicated. They know that the United States has entered into an alliance with the nationalist government in Formosa. They know that air bases will be made available to the United States, and it is an elementary step in logic that if Formosa is a threat to Chinese security these bases have to be destroyed.
We are facing the irresistible force and the immovable object, and if they both persist in following the same path they have been pursuing in recent months then tragedy may ensue. But if sanity supervenes the situation might be saved. If it does not, with what are we faced? There might be in the United States conception a war of survival, because I do not believe that a war over the offshore islands can be a limited war. I do not believe that a war between two major powers can be a limited war. Once it starts, it goes, and it goes completely. However, I offer this opinion. I do not think there is going to be war over these islands, because I think there is a growing revulsion among the people

of the United States against it, despite the fact that there are those near the top of the administration who perhaps would be willing to indulge in such a dreadful venture. But the feeling of the people of the United States is communicating itself to those in authority and that, combined with the fact that the President knows what war means, may be our greatest safeguard.
Nevertheless there are those in the United States-and again those in high positions-[DOT] who are willing to see us go to war over these offshore islands. Perhaps they have not followed out the logic of their thoughts. If they did, I submit, they would arrive at a picture as black as it is possible to paint. If the United States decides that the security of Formosa depended upon the offshore islands, they will fight for those offshore islands. The Chinese maintain that they are Chinese territory; I agree. They are going to try to take them.
The question is, how will the United States conduct such a war? We have been told on high authority that if the coastal batteries in China fire, as of course they will fire, on the offshore islands, these coastal batteries will have to be obliterated. It would not only be the coastal batteries that would fire on the islands. Surely aircraft would be used also. Therefore the bases from which these aircraft come would have to be wiped out, but how would it be done?
I think all we can do is study with some care the statement made by the vice president of the United States in a speech he made in Chicago on the 17th of March of this year, according to the report in the Montreal Gazette:
Vice-president Richard M. Nixon today warned the Chinese communists in the bluntest of terms they will be met with atomic weapons if they embark upon "an additional aggression".
This is the vice president of the United States.
"It is foolish", he said, "to talk about the possibility that the weapons which might be used in the event a war breaks out in the Pacific would be limited to the conventional Korean and world war II types of explosives. We are not prepared to fight that kind of war. Our forces could not fight an effective war in the Pacific with those types of explosives if they wanted to."
That is the word of the vice president of the United States, one who but for the grace of God might conceivably be president if the present incumbent should die in office. If the Americans decide to use atomic weapons on China the result for the Chinese will be terrible. The result for the Americans will be devastating, for all that will result will be that all of Asia will be united emotionally behind China.
External Affairs
Asia has not forgotten the atomic bombs which were dropped on an Asian country. I think many Asians are still aware, as we are, that in 1945, the Americans had broken the Japanese code. In July, 1945, the Americans knew that the Japanese, through the instrumentality of Molotov and Moscow, were putting out feelers for peace. They knew that all that was stopping the Japanese from suing for peace were the terms of unconditional surrender. In July, 1945, the Japanese were virtually beaten. After July, 1945, atomic bombs were dropped in Asia, specifically in Japan.
Asians have not forgotten; neither, I think, have we. But if we take the word of the vice president of the United States, atomic bombs will be used in a new war. The Chinese after all are human beings, as we are, and they will have a desire to hit back. They will have a desire for revenge, and we would be living in a fool's paradise if we dreamt for a moment that they had not a stockpile of their own atomic weapons, not necessarily made in China but supplied to them by their friends in the Soviet union. We might be careless were we to assume that the air force the Chinese have is such that they do not have long-range bombers; and if they have long-range bombers, even though they can fly only on a one-way mission, and if they have an atomic weapon, I suspect that they will be strongly tempted to use it.
The quickest and easiest way would be over the north, where we have radar screens which may be sufficiently adequate to spot hostile planes, although I am quite sure that visual observations would be used to check the situation. The moment hostile planes are known to be flying over North America or over the Canadian north every American station across the world is alerted. We also know that; and when the situation comes, apart from the fact that our own skies will be darkened with interceptors, it only needs one blunder for the instruments of death to be launched on their way.
In a modern war one does not attack cities, one does not attack industries, one attacks airfields from which opposing aircraft can take off. I am quite sure that the Americans have many Soviet airfields pinpointed, but I am quite sure there are many which the Americans and we know nothing of, and if the final tragedy happened I am certain there would be reciprocity of the worst kind, which would mean thermonuclear war. I do not think it will happen, but it conceivably could, and it could happen this year unless sanity prevails.

External Affairs
As I said earlier, I do not believe there can be a local war between two great powers. But suppose the United States, even in a localized war, finds itself in conflict with China; what is the position of American troops in this country? After all, what is the position of belligerent troops in a neutral country? What would we do? Would we intern them or would we hand them over or convey them to the border and set them free in the United States, or have we a new concept of neutrality, as I think we have- all help to our allies short of manpower? That is a hypothetical question which may not need to be answered; nevertheless, even assuming that wisdom prevails and there is a withdrawal from the offshore islands, the problem is not solved.
One of the things which obsess many in the state department is the fear that the United States will be regarded as a paper tiger. To some extent it is a sign of immaturity, but it is a definite fear on their part. If they come to be regarded as a paper tiger the only answer I can give is that their blundering diplomacy has brought about the situation. Yet I would sooner see the United States regarded as a paper tiger than think that Canadians should have to go and fight for United States blunders.
But there is another fear, namely that the morale of Chiang Kai-shek's troops on Formosa will be hurt or will perhaps be ruined if we give up these offshore islands. Again I answer quite simply that I would sooner see that morale totally destroyed than see one Canadian killed fighting for Chiang Kai-shek and Formosa. As far as we are concerned in this party, not only are we not prepared to support any war for the offshore islands, but we will not support any sort of war for Formosa as long as Chiang Kai-shek is there. If there is any validity in what the Minister of Trade and Commerce says, then there is going to be a fight in this country; because we will fight this issue not only within parliament but in every area across Canada.
We have no business getting into a war to protect Chaing Kai-shek and his admirals and his generals in Formosa. If Chiang Kai-shek is not an interloper in Formosa, that means that Formosa is Chinese territory. We have no right getting into a Chinese civil war. If he is an interloper I see no reason why we should have to fight for him. The internationalization of Formosa has been asked for. That may be a solution. But Chiang Kai-shek must be removed. I am not going to say that he should be put on a modern Elba, but perhaps the China lobby in the United States could
IMr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).]
act as host to him for an indeterminate time. At least let us take him out of circulation in the Pacific area.
One thing the minister asked us to do was to try to find out what the Asian objectives are. Premier Chou En-lai some months ago said this:
Unless we establish a powerful modern industry, a modern agricultural system, modern communications and transport services, and a modern national defence we will not be able to shake off our backwardness and poverty.
I think what Chou said would be accepted by most Asians. They are determined to achieve equality, and with every justification in the world. They are tired of being treated as subject people-as coloured people. We talk-and I have the unhappy feeling that we do so disparagingly-of the coloured people in Asia. Mr. Speaker, white is also a colour. In our own way we are just as much coloured people. Also we cherish our religion of Christianity. I am sure they cherish their own faith in precisely the same way we cherish ours.
A year ago I spoke in debate at the time of the meeting in Geneva, and I referred to the desire of the Asians to be rid of colonialism, their desire to be free and their desire for equality as well. In the opinion of the Asians the only way this equality can be manifested is through a vast program of industrialization throughout the various countries. The Asians are going to decide their own destiny. They are going to choose their own friends. The less we have to do with deciding their destiny, except in a co-operative way, the better it will be. We must realize that revolution is going to be the order of the day for many years in Asia but we should realize also that revolution of that sort can conceivably be quite bloodless. Yet we are afraid of revolution. We who are the creatures, the children of revolution are desperately afraid of seeing it in other places. Let me quote this:
In fostering revolutions wherever they show themselves, in regretting those which have failed, in extending a helping hand to those which seem to prosper, they lend new strength to the apostles of sedition and reanimate the courage of every conspirator.
That is not a statement by some member of the state department about the Soviet union. It was spoken 140 years ago by Count Metternich and he was describing the United States, and quite rightly so, because America was then trying to grow into nationhood. She had had a revolution. The revolution was essential to her nationhood and her well-being. Now we are unfortunately reaching the position that the United States and many others wish to deny this right to Asia. It is amazing how soon the most

ardent revolutionaries become the staunchest supporters of the status quo. We ought to remember that we are all the children of revolution, and that if other countries want to indulge in the same practice they should be allowed to go to it.
Furthermore, we had on this continent 140 years ago what was known as the Monroe doctrine, which worked, due in part to the tacit approval of England. What would happen if the Asian nations decided they were going to have their own particular Monroe doctrine in Asia? What then would we think? Would we think they are criminal or venal and that they must be stopped, or do we concede to them the right which we ourselves have?
There is just now going on a meeting at Bandung which all of us are watching with the greatest interest. I do not expect too much from it, but it may be significant. I do not expect too much because there are many disparate and diverse elements there. There are many conflicts of ideologies. There are perhaps those who aspire to take over the leadership of Asia and who find themselves in conflict with others.
Agreement will be difficult on various matters, but agreement that colonialism must stop will be unanimous. Agreement that there must be the greatest measure of freedom for the people of Asia will be unanimous. Agreement that the standards and conditions of the people in Asia must be raised will be unanimous, because it is disgraceful to think that human beings in Asia who, by our Christian doctrine are the children of God, have a life expectancy of some 27 years. They know nothing but poverty. To expect them to share our fight against communism is to ask far too much of them. What we must be careful about is this. We must not try to draw our specifications for Asia. Let them draw their own blueprints. Let them have their own plans to fit their own needs. Then by all means let us go in and help them. But above all let us help them in every way possible toward achieving that equality of status which they themselves want.
However, one task beggars the imagination. By and large the village is the communal basis of life. It is true that there are cities, but there are not many of them in comparison with the number of villages. The village is the centre of life. It is the centre of the religious beliefs of the people. Their headman is in the village. The local priest is in the village. They have village discipline. There are village mores. There is a sense of belonging, a sense of community, in the village. There is also starvation.
External Affairs
There is also a subsistence level of which the people in Asia are determined to rid themselves.
If industrialization on a large scale is going to start in Asia, there is going to be an efflux from these villages into the towns. We remember the human havoc created by the Occidental industrial revolution. That havoc will be nothing compared to the human havoc which will be wreaked in the Orient unless the west is prepared to come to their assistance. It will be the sort of social havoc in which communism will breed unless the west is prepared to come to the assistance of the various countries. Asia is determined to go ahead with its industrial revolution. The people know the chances which must be taken. They are prepared and determined to take those chances. They are going to need capital, obviously. They are going to need long-range education. They are going to need improvements not only in the myriad of villages but in the cities; I refer to improvements in the way of health, sanitation, and the building of hospitals. They are going to need help in the techniques of industry.
I think that is where the west can play a significant part. With the help of our artisans, craftsmen and social welfare workers, our doctors and our nurses, we must be prepared to place at their disposal whatever resources we have when they request them. But they need capital. There is so little capital because there is so much poverty. After the last war the Russians accumulated capital by fastening on their people a most repressive regime in which life did not count so long as there were savings arising out of production, which savings could be channelled into industrialization. Conceivably, that will happen to Asians, unless they are helped. Those nations which are able to help are the ones which have savings like those of us in the west, savings which must be invested and which could be invested in no better way than in helping to improve the standard of living of the Asian people. We shall have to be prepared to support land reform, no matter how obnoxious some of us may find it.
I am afraid we shall have to encourage nationalism. I never for a moment thought that I would encourage nationalism. I do not like it. Nevertheless, Asia is going through a period through which the western nations went 100 years ago. Nationalism is in the air in Asia, and what I fear is that the Asian people will absorb our vices without at the same time assuming our virtues. But it is a stage through which they are going, and therefore we had better realize it. We ought to be doing all we can to assist them. The great

External Affairs
problem is going to be that they are not going to take 100 years to achieve their hoped for equality through industrialization; they are going to try to do it in a generation if they possibly can. Earlier, I mentioned very briefly some of the problems which would be faced. The minister knows them. The minister has said that all sorts of aid must be extended to Asia, and still we give this miserable $25 million per year through the Colombo plan, and a smattering of dollars here and a smattering of dollars somewhere else.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: Oh, but they are raising it to $26 million.

speechtext: They are raising it to $26 million, but if they raised it to $260 million it would be a lot better. In the last few years we have spent billions of dollars on antiquated, outmoded and archaic forms of defence.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: So have the Asian countries.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They may have, but we would have had much more defence had we used some of these hundreds of millions of dollars to do the things which the minister himself said should be done.
One of the obvious things to do is to provide, in part, the capital assistance which is required in Asia. But I do not want to see it done on a national basis. If it is going to be done properly, if it is going to be done successfully, it has to be done through the United Nations. There is no other way. Any one nation doing it on an individual basis is going to be suspect, human nature being what it is. The United States people were generous in the Marshall plan. The recipients of that aid have no greater love today for the United States than they had before the Marshall plan. The Marshall plan has helped them greatly as anyone can see from the European statistics on industrial production. But this has to be done collectively through the United Nations, as was suggested a few years ago. At that time a special United Nations fund for special economic development was suggested, with a request for an opening capital of $250 million. What was the position of Canada? Our commitments for defence were too heavy; we could not afford it. Instead of spending some of these tens of millions of dollars on outdated conventional weapons, which no longer are within the ambit of the new rules of war, would it not have been far better to use that money to help the nations of Asia economically and in other ways? But no; this government will not do it.
The minister will speak about it. The minister has the country completely confused. [Mr. Stewart (Winnioee North).!
Canadians believe we are giving away hundreds of millions of dollars a year on the basis of the minister's speeches, yet on the basis of the government's action we are giving away an amount which is quite close to peanuts when we consider the need in the world. We have to help, but we have to help by understanding them. That is what the Asian people want. They want to choose their own leaders. They do not want to have reactionaries imposed upon them, as has been the case in the past. They do not want the Chiang Kai-sheks; they do not want the Bao Dais; and I doubt if many really want the Syngman Rhees. Their leaders must have the confidence of the people. It is conceivable we shall dislike their policies immensely, but so long as they have the support of the people we have to realize that if there are elected leaders in Asia who are going to carry on this fight against communism in their own way it will pay us to support them. It will not pay us to support them in the sense that we are in a position of sovereignty over them. We should support them on the basis of a partnership. We should support them on the basis of mutual aid.
The alternative is plain if we do not do it. The Asians will prefer their own form of communism to western imperialism. I do not think there can be any question whatever about it. The Asians have shown they can solve their own problem. All one has to do is to consider what happened in the state of Andhra in India, some few weeks ago, a state of some 20 million people, which all the commentators told us was threatening to go communist. When I read in Time magazine that this was the case I felt greatly encouraged because Time is lamentably wrong in most of these cases. What happened was that, although the communists pulled every trick out of the bag, nevertheless Mr. Nehru managed to so sway and arrange affairs that the communists were thoroughly trounced. This was done without any help at all from the state department, miraculous as that may seem. Really, I think the Asians are quite capable of solving their other problems in the same way if they get some help.
All I say is this. We cannot make allies of these people by asking them to join in the fight against communism. We are going to make allies by asking to join with them in a partnership in the fight against poverty and disease which has so afflicted them, and which is so implicit in the minister's speech but which is denied so explicity by government policy. We see what the anti-communist regimes can do in India, in Burma and in Indonesia, but there are others who need our help. What we have to realize is

that the fight in Asia is not between western ideas and communism; it is not between western standards and communism; it is not between western economics and communism; it is not between western capitalism and communism. It is a fight against poverty. Until we realize that, and until we are prepared to play our part in combating that poverty, we are going to continue to lose out.
I believe the time has come when the western powers have to make up their minds exactly what they are going to do in Asia. We cannot be the victims all the time of the policies of the United States which leave us confused and unhappy, not knowing what is to be done. There is one good thing to be said for the actual fact of United States policy, it is providentially a far different thing from the numberless policies which are given out and emitted by the brass hats in the Pentagon and the would-be Warwicks in the state department and in other positions of influence in the United States. United States policy in action has fortunately been far different from the suggestions which have been made by the leading exponents of policy in that country.
So, what we have to do is to assure the Asians that it is our objective to see that they are freed from foreign domination and that they have leaders of their own choice. We should show them we are prepared to co-operate with them in every way possible to raise their standards of living, socially and economically. The alternative is plain. The alternative is years of stress, perhaps not years of terror, but years of alarms and excursions and threats, leaving some more and more despondent and others more and more despairing.
I was reading a book of Lewis Mumford's the other day, and he quoted a letter from a correspondent which went as follows:
Each culture evolves a characteristic gesture that symbolizes its essential values. Thus Christianity brings to mind a suppliant figure on its knees in prayer; the Buddha sits in the calm ot eternity with snails in his hair. The gods and Pharaohs are seated-great granite figures of power. There is in these postures an element of the ultimate, an expression of a transcendent attitude.
But what, pray, is our posture upon having miraculously touched the innermost sources of nature's power? Our school children here in the backwoods of my village are taught in daily drill to duck under their desks when they hear the syren blow. The citizenry here built themselves deep underground shelters where they are to cower while their civilization is blown to atoms. And those not fortunate enough to grovel in fear and trembling underground are taught to fall upon their faces in the gutters of their cities and await their doom. Prostrate, our heads deep in the mud, we face the future. Such is our posture.
If we were to accept that, then we would believe we were moving inexorably toward
External Affairs
extinction. And it may be so; but I do not believe it. Obviously this letter is written by one who has become disillusioned, and in turn whose disillusionment has led to despair. Disillusionment might be a good thing; within limits it certainly is. But I see today no rhyme or reason for despair if we do the things we know we ought to be doing. I have no sense of despair, but I have a sense of frustration and a sense of anger. I am angry with a government which, by its blindness and by its refusal to act, by denying its own minister's policy, may perhaps save itself dollars, but conceivably could help to lose a civilization.

Mr. Speaker, usually I find myself in large measure in agreement with the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). I do not disagree with a good deal of what he said today; but on one point I think surely, upon reflection, he must realize that he was on very weak ground. That was when he asked, what would we do in the event of war, if the United States was in that war and Canada was not? He asked whether we in Canada would intern Americans, or what we would do.
I am sure my hon. friend, who is such a strong supporter-as I am-of NATO, must realize that NATO is the last solid device we have in this world today, apart from the political device of the United Nations, to protect our security. I am sure the hon. member must realize, upon reflection, that he was talking directly contrary to the set-up of NATO. Of course if the United States got into a war, and Canada did not, the uniformed forces stationed in Canada or in any other part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization area would have every legal right to remain there, and to operate there.
I think, too, if my hon. friend will look back in history he will see that there have been other great historic occasions when one part of the world was engaged in war and another part was not; and yet that did not compel the part of the world that was not technically at war to apply all of the technicalities of neutrality.
I think my hon. friend will remember that when the two great world democratic leaders, Winston Churchill and Franklin Delano Roosevelt, met on a battleship at their historic conference off Newfoundland, there was no attempt on the part of the United States naval forces to intern that person who called himself "naval person", simply because he happened to be wearing the uniform of the British navy.

External Affairs
And when I am on the subject of Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Mr. Churchill may I say that I am glad to see in this debate, unlike the debate that took place on the same subject on February 12, 1953, members of the Social Credit party have not taken quite so anti-Roosevelt a position as they did then, when the leader of that party said, as reported at page 1881 of Hansard:
But, Mr. Speaker, when the full history of these times is written, when all of the facts have been brought to light, there will be many people who will say that the past two presidents of the United States have been the great betrayers of humanity.
In my opinion that was one of the most unfortunate statements ever made in any British parliament; because if the people of the British commonwealth ever owed a great debt to one personality, they owed it to that very great Democrat, the late Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Nowadays, when it is the fashion to debunk so many people and to besmirch and belittle so many people, and with people making a lot of money debunking persons such as Lawrence of Arabia, and when people can make money by making offhand comments about what was said or supposed to have been said at the Yalta conference, I wish to say that in my opinion we never would have come through the great world crisis, and we would not be here today debating how to deal with this latest menace with which the free world is faced, had it not been for the great support we got from that greathearted Democrat, the late Franklin Delano Roosevelt-even for years before the United States was technically in the war.

He said something the other day to the effect that perhaps we should try gestures of good will to these 600 million people of China, that perhaps we should even give them some gifts of our surplus wheat, and see how they would react to that.

I am not suggesting that is a practical proposition; but when I compare the spirit of that statement with the spirit of what we heard this afternoon from my very good friend, for whom I have a warm feeling in my heart, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), then I think I would have to go along with Mr. Orvis Kennedy and not with the hon. member for Lethbridge.
When I hear these fulsome flatteries, these fulsome compliments, to Chiang Kai-shek- and I for one will not say one word in disparagement of Chiang Kai-shek or, for that matter, any other Chinese statesman today- I think that sometimes it is an advantage to have held a job for a long time. I happen to have been in newspaper work in Canada for 33 years, and my memory goes back to some of the very first articles I wrote. These were in the years when Chiang Kai-shek was winning southern China. I think I could even dig up some of the old scrap-books; and if I dug up scrap-books and photographs I am sure I would find the Russian adviser, General Borodin, or General Galen, standing side by side with Chiang Kai-shek in the conquest of southern China. And I think if I were to dig up another news item I would find that in February 1943 I wrote an article for many Canadian newspapers stating that there was a state of disguised civil war in China between the forces of Chiang Kai-shek and those of communism.
One of my most prized souvenirs is a letter I received on the official letterhead of the consul general of China in Canada demanding a published retraction in Vancouver papers, and saying that there was never anything so nonsensical as trouble between the communists and the government of Chiang Kai-shek. And so I say that sometimes it is an advantage to have a long memory and to have had an experience in these times through which we are passing.
I intervene in the debate today to make only a few points. I wish first to compliment the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) upon what I thought was one of the most masterly exhibitions of practical diplomacy I have been privileged to see. And if we want to know what a masterly exhibition of practical diplomacy it was, all we have to do is to see what has happened subsequently in the United States. When I saw the technique of the Secretary of State for External Affairs first in his Toronto speech and also in this house, I wondered to myself just what he was doing, and then afterwards I thought I saw the point exactly. I thought that he made the most important point of all, and perhaps he made it first, namely, that in any life and death struggle, whether

we like it or not, we are indissolubly tied in with the United States. Whether we like it or not, in any such life and death struggle involving the United States and Canada, involving in practical terms, if we want it that way, the areas of northern Canada or any other part of the North Atlantic treaty area, which we are obliged to defend, we would be in that war from the first day and from the very first hour. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we cannot too lightly take the view that anything that is happening out in Asia does not immediately concern us, even if, as the minister pointed out, we may have no direct commitments, or no immediate obligations for what happens there. I say that if we ever wanted proof that Canada counts when she speaks out in international affairs or, in a larger sense, that the British commonwealth counts when it speaks, either publicly or privately, to make peace, we have seen that demonstrated in the past month or six weeks.
We have seen a great modification of the United States policy, particularly in regard to those two disputed offshore islands of Quemoy and Matsu. The minister made very clear, not only on that occasion but on other occasions, that Canada believes they belong to or they are part of the Chinese mainland. These, of course, are my own words. It would be the height of folly to have a war over those two particular islands; but there is a quite different situation in regard to the larger disputed island of Formosa.
If we are to make our influence felt in international affairs, perhaps we should be prepared to speak out just as clearly on Formosa as Canada has already spoken out on the offshore islands. I for one sincerely hope that either Canada or some other member of the British commonwealth takes the initiative at the proper time to see that there is something in the nature of a United Nations trusteeship set up over the island of Formosa for a fixed number of years. I would suggest not too short a period; I would suggest about ten years. It seems to me that if we are to make our voice felt, even as practical peacemakers, we have to suggest something that takes into account the actual realities of the world in which we live, and one of the realities in the world in which we live is that, regardless of the legal or even moral position of the ultimate ownership of the island of Formosa, it is a position which, in the opinion of the responsible heads of the United States military, naval and air forces, is of considerable strategic value. I for one would not be too forward, or too brash, in suggesting to the United States that they should simply wash their hands of Formosa at a time when the 50433-193J

Russian communist powers are in fact in an even more dubious position of legality in their occupation of the numerous countries of eastern Europe, including Poland, Hungary, Rumania, Bulgaria, and so on. But if we are to make a practical suggestion that has any chance of being accepted by the different contending parties, it might come out of this United Nations trusteeship idea. A United Nations trusteeship would fulfil the primary strategic objective of the United States military leaders. That objective has been stated by President Eisenhower himself, who said that they will fight, if necessary, to keep Formosa from falling into unfriendly hands.
A United Nations trusteeship would above all be fair to the people who live on the island of Formosa, and we could at least apply that principle of self-determination about which we have heard so often, as early as the first world war. Finally, I think a United Nations trusteeship might even get the agreement of the present communist government of China, because that government must know very well that if it comes to a fight they have no chance to take the island by force from the United States, if the United States wishes to try to protect it. Therefore I submit, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps Canada could make known in one way or another that she would solidly support a United Nations trusteeship for Formosa, and that it should be a stipulated number of years, and that at the end of that time the people of Formosa, in complete freedom, should be allowed to decide their own destiny.
If I understand correctly some of the subterranean half-interruptions that I hear from the other side, I might surmise that someone is saying, well, that is exactly what Mr. Attlee said in Vancouver last Saturday night. I now wish to turn for a minute, Mr. Speaker, to one other subject. The most important fact stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his two speeches on major foreign policy was that, whether we like it or not, we are inextricably bound to the United States in any war involving the life and death of our two countries. Because we are, because that is one of the facts of life that we must accept, because it is true, Mr. Speaker, that if Russian planes ever do come across the north pole and are detected by that northern distant early warning radar alarm, or by any considerable number of the many tens of thousands of people whom we have already enlisted in the ground observer corps, we know perfectly well that, regardless of any formality, the war would be on, the whole thing would be automatic. The retaliatory forces would take off from this country and that would be it. But because it is a fact of life that we are inextricably bound with the United States, we have to exercise very real forethought and great foresight to prevent complications of our position.
I am not now going to refer to the many speeches and writings of the late Colonel McCormick of the Chicago Tribune; but there are people in the United States who have queer ideas as to the future of this North America. Among them has been my very good friend, a very fine gentleman, the new junior senator from the state of Oregon, Mr. Richard Neuberger, who only a couple of weeks ago in Canadian papers from coast to coast advocated what I would call the annexation of this country to the United States, which I thought had passed out with the Tories in the year 1849, when they stoned the governor general. Incidentally, I have always blamed them for doing that as otherwise the capital would have been in Montreal and not in Bytown or Ottawa where Queen Charlotte never fixes the potholes until tuliptime, and apparently this year there is going to be a great scarcity of tulips. As I say, this thesis of annexation went out with the time the Tories stoned the governor general in 1849. We have now had it resurrected from two different ends of the scale.
It is one of the facts of life in the world in which we live that the northern frontier of Canada will have to be defended much more strongly than it is being defended today. I for one want to make my voice heard just

as clearly as I can that I am in favour of Canadians defending Canada. I am in favour of taking over the major responsibility, I do not say the entire responsibility, for defending the north of Canada. It is a fact that among the NATO powers we have become, in the famous words of Mr. Churchill, mixed up together for the common good. But I do say that we should take over the major responsibility for defending the north of Canada, that we should take whatever steps are necessary to see that the major job of defending that North American frontier is discharged by Canadians and with Canadian principles and Canadian policies in mind.
I for one would not want to give the false impression that I am in favour of bringing home from Europe any part of the strong air force we have there defending the western frontier. I had the privilege last autumn of visiting NATO headquarters in Paris and talking with one of the finest Americans I have ever met in all my life, General Nord-stad. Sometimes when we over here on this side of the border listen to the radio or read the press, and sometimes wonder about some of the things the United States might be considering doing, if we had a chance to talk with a real American like General Nordstad we would come away with a great feeling of reassurance. You know that you could trust your life with that man; you know he would never give any order that you would not give yourself if the fate of the two countries was at stake.
When I see that we have very large forces stationed in Europe and when I read that strong pressure is being exerted by some quarters to station greatly increased forces in northern Canada and that there is some suggestion that perhaps if we have not enough Canadian forces to go around we should station a large percentage of United States forces in northern Canada, I for one am completely opposed to that suggestion.
I believe that Canada should be defended by Canadians. If we have not enough air force or enough ground troops to discharge all of our obligations, it would be better at the proper time and in the proper way to transfer some of the forces which we now have in Europe, have them take over the job of sentry duty in the north and have them replaced by United States troops which some people are now suggesting should be sent to defend our northern frontier.
While I am on the subject may I say that in my opinion the time is coming when we will have to have considerably more ground forces. I for one would like to see this

country experiment a bit and I have a suggestion to make to my very honoured colleague, the minister of defence, of whom I think all British Columbia is so proud at his having been given this big and onerous job, which he is doing so well. I should like to suggest to my colleague the minister of defence and to his colleagues in the cabinet that consideration should be given to a modification of an old plan that was used as early as the first world war.
I should like to see, beginning with November 1 each year, a period of training started for perhaps 20,000, 30,000 or even 40,000 of our young men. During the past few weeks I have been checking with people whose military judgment I respect and who should know about these things. They tell me that the proper kind of intensive training would turn out very useful soldiers after a six-months codrse. I for one would like to see this experiment tried.
I think one reason why many of our young men are not joining the armed forces is the length of the period of service. Not long ago I checked to find out why more men were not joining the R.C.M.P. and the reply I got was, "Who wants to sign up for five years?" The same argument might be used with regard to the armed forces.
In any event I throw out the suggestion that Canada should consider a new way of raising and training the military forces which are going to be necessary if we are to have the increased protection which we need on our northern frontier. Let Canada be defended by Canadians. Every winter we should train several scores of thousands of young Canadians from November 1 until April 1 or May 1; they should be put through an intensive course of training. Then those who desire to be released to return to their regular civilian jobs could be released, while those who wanted to come back the following year to be fitted into a more professional or highly trained integrated unit would have that opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to make a modest contribution to this debate for the purpose of expressing my point of view and asking: where is communist ideology leading us? My intention is to use the English language for the benefit of the majority of the members of the house and I hope sympathy will be extended to me for doing so. If I should make mistakes during the course of my remarks I am sure the indulgence of hon. members will be on a par with my efforts.
As I said, where is communist ideology leading us? Owing to an intensive propaganda, carefully and hypocritically prepared,
External Affairs
too large a number of human beings, amongst whom unfortunately too many Canadians, consciously or not, and through naivete, ignorance or malice, seem to convince themselves each day, and more and more, that communism is nothing more than a political party which it is possible to join.
Thus indoctrinated, these people hope for the advent of communism to the government of their respective countries because in their ignorance and steeped in the false concepts of this fatal doctrine they look forward to the quick healing of the ills with which they are afflicted and the end of the miseries afflicting them.
On the other hand, the leaders of this pernicious ideology, reactionaries through hate or disposition, harassed with the idea of dominating, materialists to the point of even denying the existence of a Supreme Being, verily believe in the administration of the world by a caste of people without soul or heart, or respect for man as a being, created by God, and they seem bent upon imposing a diabolical dictatorship which would make slaves of the free men of today. Let us not fool ourselves. Communism is not a political party in the real sense of the word, for its doctrines are not founded upon principles of social and economic order. Its bases lack this conception of democracy to which each and every one of us is so deeply rooted. Moreover, it does not have this definition which we have of the democratic regime which, freely chosen by the people, must apply itself to serve the people.
On the contrary, communism is a movement of ideas. It is a complete denial of the rights of the collectivity. Its ideology is a new concept of the world and life, embracing atheistic materialism and denying the existence of all spiritualism. Its leaders and partisans consider it as a pseudo-religion.
Since the end of world war II, out of which the democratic countries emerged victorious, without having obtained peace, the communists, our allies in the victory over the nazi hordes, did not lose any time in invading certain countries which they dominate today, and which are administered by governments selected and approved by the Kremlin, the undisputed centre of communism in the world.
Feeling powerful after the help given the democracies in their fight against Hitler's Germany, and attributing the victory to themselves, without delay they started the conquest of certain countries hitherto democratic, employing, for so doing, their skilful propaganda as well as the methods and the arguments best suited to each centre.

External Affairs
At this point, I would like to make a digression and state that in certain countries they have exploited the miseries and the poverty of the people. We should not forget that poverty gives birth to communism and the best action to be taken to prevent it in Canada is to administer in such a way that every Canadian can have the job he is entitled to and in the meantime be kept away from starvation.
I will always remember what the Italian prime minister said at the national press club in Washington during his last trip there, that the "communist element in his country grew from economic, not ideological causes". At the same time Premier Scelba expressed his nation's gratitude for "generous and spontaneous aid" from the United States, without which, he said, neither Italy nor the rest of Europe could have avoided calamity.
We in Canada are also contributing our fair share in the economic recovery of certain nations with the aim, no doubt, of preventing communism from finding its way into those populations. I therefore do not hesitate to repeat that we are thus making a great humanitarian gesture and that we will have contributed in large measure to upholding the democratic system within those nations, a symbol of peace, justice and future prosperity.
However, we must not forget that misery and poverty have both made their sorrowful appearance in our country and that we owe it to ourselves to do everything possible in order to prevent its disastrous spreading. I also reiterate that Canada's contribution to the member nations of the Colombo plan must be maintained and increased, if possible, but on the condition only that we concern ourselves about our own citizens at least in the very same measure as we do with respect to outsiders.
Communism cunningly filters into all classes, and we cannot allow ourselves to live in this country in a culpable lethargy. Let us only remember the sad examples of Poland, Czechoslovakia and many other countries today living in bondage in Moscow, thus pointing to the fact that the leaders of those days did not foresee the menace that was threatening them and unfortunately became a reality.
Referring to communist propaganda again, I wish to say that to the peaceful propaganda were added the forceful means, the massacres and persecutions, such as we have read accounts of in the free press for a few years and which are the satanical means suggested by Marx himself in the conquest of the world into bolshevik slavery. It matters little what dishonest and damnable means communism must use to attain its aim in the

domination of the world; what really counts is the intended objective. It is the enforcement afterwards of a universal rule which will enslave the free man, establishing a materialistic and atheistic policy, which ignores the authority of our Creator, God, of men and things, but forces the human world to adore the new masters of the world, the eventual successors to Lenin and Stalin.
The communists entertain the hope-I should say that they are assured-that little by little, and maybe sooner than we could imagine it ourselves, the Marxist way of thinking will penetrate all our minds, and that it will acquire the freedom of the cities. If no dike is built against communism, we shall soon note that the people think in a Marxist way, meaning before everything that they have become totally materialistic and atheistic.
Numerous have been those in the world who sacrificed themselves on the altar of well-understood democracy in the course of the two world wars and who have made the supreme sacrifice so that this democracy founded on real peace, justice, entente cor-diale, brotherly love and faith in God may live and endure. If at this moment we cast a look into the painful situation in which those who long for peace and liberty find themselves, we must come to the conclusion that the time is serious and we cannot afford to dismiss lightly the constant menace overhanging our heads, and that we cannot possibly remain indifferent to the continued threats of attack by force of the Chinese communists engaged by their masters from the Kremlin. The idea of domination by soviet Russia is becoming more and more concrete, and the sudden changes which took place recently within the soviet supreme command fairly indicate that the promoters of disunity and war have won a nefarious and dangerous victory for the security of the world.
Their Chinese satellites, obeying blindly Moscow's orders, are thus getting ready to launch on Formosa and its adjacent islands an armed attack of which the main aim is to incite the United States to make reprisals in order to keep that strategic centre, necessary to its defence and still occupied and fortified by Chiang Kai-shek's nationalists.
A retort from our powerful allies and neighbours would undoubtedly throw all the nations of the world into a war, since at that very moment a Russia well armed and in readiness for quite a few long years would already be in the fray behind red China, dragging along with her all those countries which she succeeded in dominating and communizing. The preparations for a conquering thrust are

going ahead at an accelerated pace in red China under the surveillance, the approval and the direction of Moscow, and from one moment to another the world will have to face that stark reality.
It will be the launching of a war aiming at the conquest of the peoples, to the benefit of a disastrous and diabolical ideology. It will be the seeding of devastation, sorrow and death. It would no doubt be the beginning of the requiem of our democratic liberties, if the communist forces were ever to emerge victorious.
Mr. Speaker, communism is heading us, little by little, towards a future which every man, ever so little serious, cannot envisage with optimism, short of finding a quick solution which would prevent the destruction of the human world.
I do not pretend to have found that solution, but it seems to me that it is open to any man, particularly to those who occupy responsible public positions, to collect himself and to search for suggestions likely to solve a problem of such importance and seriousness.
In the manner of Christians, which we are, we believe that God and God alone was the Maker of man and things, and that it belongs to Him only to determine the end of things and human beings.
We can entertain different views as to the means we should take to avoid an international struggle which would bring into conflict nations having widely opposed ideologies, and on the strategy to follow in order to ensure our defence.
In the light of facts and circumstances we must, however, not forget that everything must be tried so as to establish peace in the world, token of happiness and prosperity: that peace which was promised by God to men of good will.
The general public, together with certain persons who hold positions of authority, do not seem to see and realize where a war, waged with the H-bomb and all similar devastating modern armaments, would lead us.
If we but remember what happened when an atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima, causing death and destruction, we shall see that an H-bomb can destroy at the same time cities of such importance and population as London, New York and Moscow.
If an H-bomb war were to be waged, it would mean that in no time at all the world would literally be wiped out. If all the inhabitants of London, New York and Moscow were to be exterminated, the world could, in centuries, rebuild, and the whole thing would be looked upon as a minor disaster, however
External Affairs
considerable it might be. But we now know, more particularly since the Bikini test, that the H-bombs can gradually spread their destructive powers over a much wider area than that the scientists had at first forecast.
It is now authoritatively recognized that one bomb can be made with a destructive power 25,000 times greater than the atomic bomb which once destroyed Hiroshima.
Such a bomb, the explosion of which takes place in the air or on the sea, has radioactive particles which spread in the air. These radioactive particles gradually reach the surface of the earth in the form of deadly dust or rain. It was with that dust that the Japanese fishermen and the fish were infected, even though they were altogether out of what the American experts considered to be the danger zone.
As yet, nobody knows just how far those radioactive particles can reach. However, the most competent authorities are unanimous in saying that a war where the H-bomb would be used could bring about the end of the human world. It is to be feared that if a great number of those bombs were used as a means of attack or defence, this would mean universal death; it would mean sudden death for a fortunate minority only, for it would mean, for the greater number, a slow death accompanied by tortures which it would be impossible to depict.
We therefore have to face a situation which deserves a care from which we cannot escape. We must make a thorough examination and ask ourselves what means to take to avoid a war, without however forgetting that we must, at all costs, stop the forever growing menace of communism in the world.
In the gospel, our Lord gave us this saying upon which every Christian should meditate and put into practice: "Love one another". He did not only give us this advice, since He gave us the example by sacrificing Himself on the cross, in His great love for the world.
More than ever before, it is high time that the nations resume the practice of that doctrine, that we follow the example which was set by our ancestors, and that the feeling of brotherly love which formerly prompted man again become the prerogative of our life and our future.
Whatever our relations may be, let us remove from them, hypocrisy, untruth, pride, the hunger for domination and love of lucre. With regard to diplomatic relations between nations, may they be founded upon frankness and honesty. Let us remember that wile and deceit last only so long, and that sooner or later those who employ those contemptible means inevitably get caught in their own snare.

External Affairs
The communists forget all about the existence of God and base their policy and desires of conquest on political data only; they cannot be imbued with love for their fellow men and are inevitably unhappy, deceitful, lying, proud and arrogant, acting only through animal instinct. Within their minds, they keep alive that hideous cancer, that ideology condemned by faith and good sense, which communism is, and of which the deadly propaganda has no other aim than to poison the heart and soul of those whom it has indoctrinated, only to kill them afterwards.
We must therefore face the following alternatives: First, the conquest of the world by anti-social, anti-patriotic, anti-Christian communism, which would turn us into beings with an animal instinct, slaves without ideals and future. We should forever say good-bye to private enterprise and to our status of free men and should renounce our glorious past and our most noble, patriotic and religious traditions. Our life would be affected by the horrors of those massacres and persecutions, the establishment of those state prisons which we call concentration camps, the infamous tortures of those people who are thirsty for blood and tears, and finally death, without the satisfaction of having near us one who would at least pray for the salvation of our souls.
Second, the gradual destruction of humankind by means of that H-bomb which by degrees would wipe out men and things, and which would make us suffer the most atrocious pains. Those sufferings would be equalled only by those endured in primeval days, when men were straining to find inconceivable ways of torturing the early Christians.
In order to avoid such a catastrophe, I can only see one solution, and without doubt the best one to protect imperilled humankind. I refer to the return to God and His teachings, through prayer, so that He may inspire the aggressors to discontinue the expansion of their subversive doctrine and prevent them from going into mass assassination of that world which He created, and that He alone has the right to annihilate.
Let us urge the leaders of our democratic nations to call upon the guidance of Providence in all their discussions. Let them call upon the guiding light of the Holy Ghost, who will enlighten them in the important decisions which they must make for the happiness, peace and security of the peoples whom they administer.
