subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When I was in Vancouver at Easter, Mr. Speaker, I was interviewed by a member of the Vancouver press and he asked me a question concerning

the attitude of the members of the House of Commons towards external affairs. He asked me if I thought the majority of the members were interested in Canada's external affairs or foreign relations. I found that question rather difficult to answer. I said that I imagined everyone in the House of Commons, like everyone else I presume who thinks at all, at least occasionally must have a few questions in his mind about our relations with the rest of the world. I was of the opinion, however, that a great many members of the house felt that they were quite uncertain as to what Canada's foreign policy actually is, and therefore they felt incapable of commenting on it, either commending it or opposing it.
There is a strange quality about Canada's foreign policy, Mr. Speaker, almost an impression that it is all done by mirrors. We have to find out what our policy is by a careful examination of the statements that are made to tell us what it is not. It is a very difficult process. In fact, sometimes I am reminded of the old Greek stories about the Delphic oracle when I listen to our minister of external affairs. You will recall that the Greeks used to go to Delphi and they used to put their questions to the Python priestess there, who came out with very cryptic answers. The devout pilgrims used to look at the answers and scratch their heads because there were two or three interpretations as to what the answer meant. I feel that for the last two or three years we have been somewhat in that position with regard to Canada's foreign policy.
Of course, the underlying basis of Canada's foreign policy, as the minister of external affairs has told us repeatedly and quite rightly, is the fact of our geographical proximity to the United States and the necessity of taking into account our relationships with that country before any other consideration. This is quite true, and it is an obvious fact. But for some time I have regretted that, beyond the formal commitments under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, our government has not really come out with a forthright statement of our intentions with regard to the United States in the event of an attack upon North America. It is true that it is implied, in fact it is stated, in the North Atlantic treaty that we shall have to go to their aid in repelling an attack on the other members of NATO, of which the United States is the major ally.
I have this feeling, that if our government were to state quite plainly and bluntly to our American friends and the rest of the world that any attack on the United States, whether through Canada, through Hawaii, California or Florida or anywhere else, would

not merely see Canada dragged in by the hair of her head, but would see Canada quite actively and at the very outset placing our entire resources behind repelling those forces, then our position would be stronger. I do not like to think of Canada as being merely the Belgium of another war. We should have a more positive stand. We should state quite plainly that we recognize that the safety of the United States is our safety. If we made that very positive then we would be in a position to speak bluntly and plainly to our United States friends when they pursued policies which to our mind are policies which may very well invite that attack which we must help them repel.
We do not do that. Instead of that, we permit ourselves to be pushed along a number of very dubious policy paths, paths that cause a great deal of concern, I am quite sure, to every member of this house including the minister of external affairs. I want to refer rather briefly to one policy decision that we made this year. I do this, not in any sense of attempting to say I told you so, but merely as an example of the danger of following a policy about which we have some misgivings. I refer to the ratification of the Paris treaties. I do not think anyone will deny that practically every member in this house had very grave misgivings, and the minister himself told us that it was with grave misgivings that he advocated this policy, but he could see no alternative. There were some of us who considered that those misgivings should have dictated our policy.
The news from Europe recently does tend to cast some doubt on the wisdom of the policy that was decided upon at that time. The news, for instance, of the negotiations between the Soviet union and Austria is, I think, very ominous because we see here exactly the pattern of the advances the Soviet union will make to West Germany. We see the very ominous prospect, Mr. Speaker, that the Russians will be prepared to offer the German people the great prize in which they are interested, that is reunification of Germany. While they will do that ostensibly on the basis of having a neutralized and disarmed Germany, and while that reunited Germany may for some time be disarmed and neutralized, we should never forget that, reunited under the auspices of the Soviet union, the eyes of the German people will be turned eastward in gratitude rather than westward, as they might have been had we taken another policy.
We paid another very heavy price in connection with that, and it is one of which we had warning. I heard of it in Europe when I was there last year. I refer to the collapse
External Affairs
of the only honest, progressive and decisive government that France has had since the end of the war; that was part of the price we paid for it, turning France back again into the hands of people who had been signally incapable of bringing France back to her previous pre-war status, to say nothing harsher about them. It was quite obvious that Mr. Mendes-Franee was able to maintain his hold over the national assembly merely because the members of the national assembly knew the nation was behind him. It was behind Mr. Mendes-Franee because of his decisive handling of the Indo-Chinese problem and his announced determination to deal with some of the worst economic evils, transferring more of the burden of the cost of administration to the shoulders of those who could best bear it, the improvement of social services for the French people and, in short, bringing order into the French economy. And he had, on account of that program and on account of that achievement in the international field, such public support that not even the rather dubious elements in the French national assembly were prepared to throw him out.
But the moment that we in the rest of the western world insisted that Mr. Mendes-Franee put his head on the block and agree to German rearmament, that popular support was cut away from him, and immediately his assembly support followed, with the result that Mr. Mendes-Franee fell. And instead of having a potentially strong and determined ally we have now another demoralized country, again struggling in the pit of political corruption which, unfortunately, has been the fate of France since the war.
This I think can be attributed to our determination to follow the predominantly American line of policy. I do not think anyone will deny it was that tremendous pressure of the United States that induced the rest of the western allies to support ratification, and I suggest we have already paid a very heavy price for it.
There is not much that can be done about it now. It is finished; it is water under the bridge. But we have now some other policy decisions to make that may very well affect future events. At this time there is a conference going on in Asia, the Bandung conference; and of course what is happening there is a test of strength between two Asiatic figures, namely Nehru of India and Chou En-lai of communist China. And the fate of Asia may very well depend upon which of those two men prevails at that conference. I, myself, am not very optimistic. I believe that Mr. Nehru, however, might well have

External Affairs
been placed in a position of being able to capture all Asiatic minds-and that is what those men are trying to do today-had we in North America devoted even a small fraction of the wealth we have devoted to defences of rather doubtful value to make a massive contribution to the capital development of India and the rest of southeast Asia. Then Mr. Nehru would have been able to offer the Asiatic peoples economic progress plus freedom.
But if he is placed in the position of merely offering them political freedom without economic progress, then Mr. Chou En-lai, who, undoubtedly, has the dictatorial power to develop China as he and his advisers wish to develop it, is going to be in a much stronger position to appeal to those people. Because of course it is a truism that if starving people are offered the choice between a loaf of bread and freedom, they will reach for the loaf of bread. And I am very much afraid that Chou En-lai has been left in a position of having more loaves in his basket than Mr. Nehru.
That is another opportunity we have missed, quite largely I think because we have not placed ourselves in the position of being able to speak bluntly and plainly to the most important figure in the western world, the United States of America, which undoubtedly has demanded that we devote an enormous part of our resources to these defences which, as I say, are of rather doubtful value in the view of military experts who presumably know what they are talking about.
However, I am not a pessimist. I do not think we will have another war. I think Sir Winston Churchill's last dictum was perhaps the most profound, when he said that the world has developed weapons which both sides are afraid to use, and that we may very well find some safety in the shadow of world annihilation.
But we then face another danger. And it is a danger that was rather neatly expressed two days ago by the medical profession of Great Britain, in a statement appearing in the Medical Press, which is the professional journal of the medical profession in that country. I wish to quote from this, as it appeared in the Globe and Mail as a reprint from Reuters in London on April 19. It says:
Atomic and hydrogen bomb tests should be halted pending international research into the genetic hazards of radiation, the Medical Press. British professional journal, said today.
"If the struggle to perfect nuclear weapons is in fact a struggle towards peace it will indeed be ironical if it produces without war the most dangerous and fearful effect which war could bring," it added.

"If in 30 years time we are told that a doubling of background radiation is in fact dangerous that information will only be of academic importance because the doubling will already have taken place and nothing can undo it".
Let us get that through our heads.
The Medical Press suggested that while some of the test explosions might be scientifically necessary others were "largely a sort of sabre-rattling".
"It is even a possibility, and not a pretty one, that there are physicists who regard these explosions with much the same sense of juvenile satisfaction as is manifest in small boys letting off homemade fireworks in the street."
I bring this up because of answers received today to questions asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The questions the hon. member placed on the order paper were as follows:
1.	Is the Canadian government giving consideration to taking the initiative in urging the United Nations to make a study as to the extent to which atomic and hydrogen bomb tests can be made without grave danger to the human race, as requested by the Federation of American Scientists?
2. If so, when will such action be taken?
3. If not, what are the reasons for the government's decision?
The answer to the first question is No-a plain and simple No. The government was not asked if it was prepared to initiate these studies. It was asked if it was prepared to take into consideration taking the initiative in urging that these studies be made. And the answer is No, that they will not do even that.
Then the second part of the question is answered by the answer given to No. 1, it states here. And then the answer to the third part-and this is the interesting part- is as follows:
The Canadian government has been in touch with friendly governments who, through the possession of atomic and thermonuclear weapons, have a direct interest in this matter. Statements made recently by responsible officials of these governments indicate that tests so far have produced a general level of radioactivity which is remote from endangering human life.
Of course these matters should be kept, and are being kept, under constant study as indicated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the house on April 4. In addition to the investigations referred to by the minister at that time, the scientific conference on the peaceful uses of atomic energy to be held in Geneva in August will consider a number of problems related to the health and safety aspects of atomic energy, including biological and genetic effects and radiation injury and protection.
The government would be prepared to support any serious studies, which gave promise of increasing our knowledge of the problem. It is the view of the government, however, that it would serve no useful purpose for it to take any special initiative at this time of the kind referred to in the question. The government will continue to consult with friendly governments on this important matter.
This is a very interesting answer, and I am sure that the Federation of American Scientists, the British Society of Nuclear Physicists

and the French Academy of Sciences, all of which have expressed concern about this, and have stated categorically that no one knows what the danger point is, will be delighted to know that the government of Canada knows what the danger point is. Because that is what the answer to this question says: They know it. Somebody has told them-
Statements made recently by responsible officials of these governments indicate that tests so far have produced a general level of radioactivity which is remote from endangering human life.
A very strange thing indeed, when the Federation of American Scientists has not yet heard of this discovery, that we have not yet reached the danger level. They tell us it has not yet been established and they are very anxious that studies should be engaged in immediately to discover that danger point. But our government is not even prepared to ask that this work be undertaken by the United Nations. Why not? The only conclusion one can come to, Mr. Speaker, is that this government is prepared to run the risk of condoning all-time, permanent genetic damage to the human race rather than offend Mr. Dulles.
There was a reference in the answer to this question to the answer given on April 4 by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). It was one of his usual extremely voluminous answers. It goes on for page after page. Here is the important part of it, as reported at page 2653 of Hansard:
Since there remain a number of unanswered questions in this field, there is a need for continuing research and investigation into the genetic problem. Increasingly large numbers of people are being exposed to increasing amounts of radiation because of the wider use of radioactive materials in industry, research and medicine. In addition, there has been a slight, though appreciable increase in radiation all over the world as a result of the weapon tests.
However, the best scientific evidence available indicates that it is most unlikely that any significant genetic effect would result from the increased radioactivity that has occurred.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare immediately send a telegram to the Federation of American Scientists, the French Academy of Sciences, and to the British Society of Nuclear Physicists, reassuring them that he has discovered what the danger point is that none of them knows anything about.
For some time, Mr. Speaker, I have been corresponding with a young French scientist, an assistant to Prince Louis de Broglie, who brought this matter to the attention of the world some months ago, and he sent me a book that he had written on the problem, which contains a foreword by a man who, of course, did not know as much about physics
External Affairs
as the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He died a few days ago. His name was Einstein, and he had this to say:
But more important still is your note on the menace to life of the cumulative action of the experimental atomic explosions. If you think I can do anything to support publicly your campaign,
I am only too ready to proffer my services.
Albert Einstein,
December 7, 1954, Princeton.
It is surely a serious state of affairs, Mr. Speaker, that our government has reached such a point that it does not even dare to ask the Americans to have a study conducted of the dangers of their program; when every responsible scientific organization in the world is telling us it is essential that that should be done.

speechtext: What my hon. friend should point out is that the Canadian government itself, through the appropriate departments, is doing the very thing that he says we are not doing.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would suggest with all due deference, Mr. Speaker, that it might be that even the officials of the minister's department would perhaps be aided in their research if they were to co-operate with the leading scientific organizations of the world which are asking that a responsible world organizational study should be instituted. I do suggest that even the most brilliant physicists in our national research council in Canada are not likely to have the opportunities available here in Canada to study the effect all over the world of the explosions that have taken place in the United States and in the Soviet union. Is he telling us that here in an area in which there have been no thermonuclear explosions our scientists can tell us more accurately the dangers than can the Federation of American Scientists, the French scientists and the British scientists? If our own government scientists are discovering some facts about the dangers of these atomic explosions, then it would seem to me the logical thing for our government to do would be to place the results of their inquiries and their investigations before an appropriate commission of the United Nations, no matter how unpopular such a course might be with the American administration, or with those sections of it who produce those statements for which there is no scientific backing whatever, none whatever, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare is well aware. As one examines his statement and the statement of his colleague of the Department of National Defence, if it were not the most serious problem in the

External Affairs
world, it would be the most ludicrous situation imaginable. We are told almost in the same breath that there is no danger, and that they do not know what the danger point is. That is the situation we are in today.
I come back to the point I made at first, namely, that unless we come out and face the world with a clear-cut statement of the serious responsibilities that we are anxious and willing to share with regard to the defence of North America and the defence of the United States, we are not going to be in a position to speak bluntly and plainly to those sections of the American administration who are now toying with these great dangers. Surely, we should seek to appeal to those very large numbers of Americans who also view their government's activities in this regard with a great deal of misgiving. Surely, we should be appealing to the American people and their sense of decency and generosity- the American people that we all know are our kind of people. Surely, we should be appealing over the heads of those irresponsible officials who are now doing their best to suppress all knowledge of this matter.
It is surely an ominous and significant thing, Mr. Speaker, when a leading body of American scientists felt it necessary to make a public statement to the world which indicated that they regarded with great fear and misgivings the activities of their own government. If our government is unprepared to take such a stand, I suppose they can console themselves with the thought that if the worst fears of those who are far more competent than I or anyone in this house are realized, there will be no one left to revile them.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset of my taking part in this debate on external affairs to pay a high tribute to Canada's role in world affairs. I feel that as a nation we have done a lot to foster the cause of world peace. I feel that our efforts under the Colombo plan, and the meeting of our obligations in full under the various agencies of the United Nations, have done much to enhance the prestige of Canada in all parts of the world.
I cannot help but remember the days before I was elected to this House of Commons. Each time that I read of the remarks our minister of external affairs made in
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo).I
various parts of the world I was glad and proud to be a Canadian with a spokesman such as that. However, it was not long before I noticed that after every progressive speech, after every speech that to me sounded like a sensible contribution to the cause of world peace, invariably when he got back to Ottawa and had a meeting either of the executive of the national Liberal advisory council or of the federal cabinet, there would ensue a speech which was so reactionary that it almost undid all the good done by the minister's original speech.
This also calls to mind the last annual meeting of the Dewdney C.C.F. association in British Columbia. As a guest dinner speaker we had a Dr. David of India. If my memory serves me right, he was the head of some theological institution in India connected with the United Church of Canada. Incidentally, Dr. David was unable to eat the dinner which was set before him because as he explained, the average Indian is unable without serious after-effects to eat such sumptuous meals as Canadians are able to prepare.
Dr. David outlined the effects of the Colombo plan. As I remember, he said that the income of the average citizen of India is $50 per year. He warned us of communist advances in India and said that if the Colombo plan, which at that time was only in its beginning, was effected as it was then conceived, it would raise the standard of living of the average citizen of India by 10 per cent. He thought that it might, and I would emphasize the "might", be able to save India from communism.
While Dr. David was speaking I had a feeling of pride in the way Canada was bearing its share under the Colombo plan. But throughout the length of his speech, whenever I thought of what we might be able to do, there arose in me a feeling of shame that we were not doing as much as we were able to do. I would remind the house that Canada's contribution under the Colombo plan is less than $2 per annum per capita as against more than $100 per capita being spent on national defence.
I should like to move on to my second subject, and that is the talk given this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). I agree with most of what the hon. member had to say, but I take serious issue with one recommendation he had to make and which seemed to me to be an advocacy of a winter army for Canada. A year ago I endorsed what the hon. member said this afternoon, that Canada's defences should be manned by Canadians and by Canadians only. I would say that this policy of Canada

for Canadians is O.K. There is nothing wrong with it as long as Canada's foreign policy is determined by Canadians. If it is to be determined in Washington, then I can see nothing wrong with Washington bearing the onus of effecting their own foreign policy. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South when he advocates that Canadians defend Canadian soil with the proviso that Canadian foreign policy be determined in Ottawa by Canadians and not by any visitors we may have in Ottawa.
I was a little leery when I heard of this idea of a winter army, lest it might be a Liberal solution to seasonal unemployment in Canada. I could not help remembering what the Conservatives did to the unemployed during the hungry thirties when they herded them into vacant army camps and looked after them there. Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver South is being a little more progressive than were the Conservatives, but he has suggested that they be herded into vacant army camps and then be given a little army exercise while there. If this is meant to be a measure of relief for seasonal unemployment, then I will oppose it most heartily.
Another member from British Columbia with whom I must take issue is the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I know that for a number of years in this house he has been urging the necessity of military preparedness as far as the west coast of Canada is concerned. I know also that he is a wholehearted supporter of a Pacific military pact. He thinks that our defences for the west coast would be much more adequately served if we did agree to a Pacific defence arrangement. Now, I think that he is completely out of touch with the sentiments of the people of British Columbia when he is advocating that policy. I think that the people of British Columbia are prepared to take their chances on world peace. Having in mind the horrible means of destruction now available, we realize that it does not much matter whether on Vancouver island we have three-inch guns or six-inch guns; we in the lower mainland will be obliterated anyway. We are not overly concerned with a Pacific military defence arrangement similar to the arrangement arrived at under NATO.
Mr. Speaker, before I continue, I should like to say that I endorse the C.C.F. policy on external affairs. My leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), has very ably put forth the C.C.F. position, its endorsement of the aims and objects of the United Nations and endorsement of the North Atlantic treaty alliance and a plea
External Affairs
for the neutralization of the island of Formosa. I believe that on other occasions he has asked our government to recognize the existing government at Peking and for the admission of red China into the United Nations. However, I feel that the world situation is much too serious for us to divide ourselves along strictly partisan lines. I feel that when the question of the survival of the human race is involved we ought, for the time of the debate at least, to forget that we are Liberals or Conservatives or members of the C.C.F. or Social Credit parties. I asked for a place on your list, Mr. Speaker, because I would like not only to endorse the C.C.F. position but also to add something to that and possibly what some of you may interpret as some qualifications to the attitude of the C.C.F. I would like to place on record why I first became a member of the C.C.F. What appealed most to me about the platform of the C.C.F. was the stand taken by our first leader, the late J. S. Woodsworth, and by one of his active supporters in this house, the late Miss Agnes Macphail. They were classed as pacifists and at that time I saw a good deal of merit in their arguments. I also recall very vividly to this house that the man who defeated the great power of the British Empire was Mahatma Gandhi, a humble man who believed in pacifism all the way down the line.
I think the Canadian people have about reached the stage where, instead of adding a million dollars for military preparedness, they feel that the Canadian government should say to a man like Dr. Schweitzer in Africa, "You are doing something for humanity; we will give you a million dollars to help you in your work", rather than change three-inch guns to six-inch guns. I think that this government would receive hearty endorsation from the Canadian people in helping this missionary, doctor and great musician. I think our history books in Canada might well be rewritten to place some emphasis on such men as he is and the work he is doing. We might place a little less emphasis on some people who are now in the light of recent inventions becoming a little old, such men as the great Lord Nelson and others like him.
Before I continue, I must at this time express my appreciation to the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne). He spoke to us, for the benefit of most of us, in the English language. I only regret that the arrangements for opposition members and the appreciation of the government toward the role of opposition members are not enough to enable members of the opposition to enjoy a little leisure time in which they might learn the other great language of this house.

External Affairs
I hope I shall be privileged to remain in this house long enough so that some day I may be able to please the hon. member for Quebec West and take my part in the debate on external affairs in his native language. I sincerely wish to compliment him on his speech, and also on almost everything he said. It was a real revelation for those of us from British Columbia-and it is not Colom-bie Canadienne; it is Colombie Britannique- we sincerely appreciated what we know was a most sincere effort on the part of the hon. member for Quebec West.
The hon. member raised some matters to which I must refer. As I said, I endorse most of what he said, but I wish to refer to his bringing the question of religion into this debate. Mr. Speaker, surely there are some Canadians who believe the Bible literally when it says "On this rock I will build my Church"; there are others of us in this house who believe the Bible just as literally when it says, "Thou shalt not kill". We think that we have the same right to believe one portion of the Good Book as other people have to believe other portions of the Good Book.

I will go further and say that I am a great believer in the supernatural, if you like. But my God does not need any sword to defend Him. He needs no hydrogen bomb. If He is a god worthy of worship, He does not need human effort at all and His rule will prevail.
Lest I be classified as an unqualified pacifist may I say at this time, as I said a year ago, that I am a firm supporter of the maintenance of law and order throughout the world. I was a believer in the league of nations. I still regret the great betrayal of the league of nations. Just for the record, let me say that it was the democracies which sabotaged the league of nations as an instrument for world peace when they failed to interfere in order to prevent aggression in the Far East and again in Abyssinia. When that happened, the common people throughout the world lost confidence in that world-wide organization.
After the last war ended, the peoples of the world decided to make another effort. I hope they will not have to make a third effort. There may be no one here to make that third effort. I feel that, in a similar way, the United Nations has been betrayed and that some of the democracies in the world today would not be overly unhappy to see the sabotage of the United Nations. At the outset let me say that I think the Soviet bloc was the first bloc-if there were blocs at that time-to betray the intent of the United Nations when they overran what are now called their satellite nations. I sometimes wonder, though, how much we helped the situation by formulating such an organization as NATO. However, if it is the only alternative to the Soviet bloc, I am in hearty support of NATO. I have voted for it in C.C.F. conventions. Yet, I should like to sound this warning. Unless we implement article 2, which I consider worthy of support on its own merits, I believe we shall run into difficulty. Article 2 is the only

insurance premium we can pay for the military aspects of NATO. Unless we are willing to pay that insurance premium, I feel that NATO will end up in disaster.
I have previously indicated my opposition to a similar alliance in the Far East in the way of a Pacific pact. I much prefer the policies pursued by the prime minister of India, namely a ruthless extermination, if you like, of communism-it will be noted that I did not say communists-within his own territory and a realistic approach to this problem of coexistence when it comes to doing business with other nations.
Many people are surprised and are expressing surprise at the lack of enthusiasm shown by Canadian youth with regard to this matter of enlistment in the army, navy or air force. Back home in my constituency there is a man who made a survey on a Saturday of all the young people whom he met. In one survey the question asked was: Would you like to become enlisted in the Canadian armed forces? The almost unanimous reply was that the young men did not know why they ought to enlist in the Canadian armed forces. Then he made another survey and the question asked was:	Would you enlist in an
armed force, under the auspices of the United Nations, designed to prevent aggression throughout the world? He claims that he had almost unanimous endorsation by all the young men he met. I think the lack of enthusiasm on the part of our young men can be explained partly by the lack of a definite Canadian foreign policy.
How do we return to the United Nations, Mr. Speaker? And return I think we must. First of all, I believe we must remember the original intent of the United Nations. The United Nations was formed to prevent aggression and not to interfere in the internal affairs of any of the member nations. If we vary from that purpose, or if we even for one moment ignore the fact that the purpose of the United Nations was to prevent aggression, then we are obliged to remember such people on our side as Marshal Tito, Syngman Rhee and Generalissimo Franco, and we are obliged to give serious thought to what right these people have to being on our side as some of us fondly like to think they are.
I think we could get back to the United Nations and its original intent if we paid a little bit more attention-and I hope our newspapers will do so-to the current Asian-African conference meeting in Indonesia. I feel that a great deal of world history is being determined there. I should like to endorse what was said by one hon. member who spoke
External Affairs
previously, namely that only now are we regretting that we in the western world did not ensure Prime Minister Nehru's being able to carry the day at this Asian-African conference. We have no one to blame but ourselves.
I notice with a good deal of worry what happened with regard to Austria. With the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) I share the worry of the whole western world as to what effect it would have on our situation if Moscow were to agree with the government of West Germany in a manner similar to that in which they agreed with the government of Austria. The government of Austria has said that in return they will remain forever neutral in the matter of military involvements. The government of Sweden has always adopted the same policy. In taking part in this debate I notice that the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew) expressed a good deal of concern about what was going to happen and about the inherent dangers in the rearming of West Germany. I feel that we are now just a little bit late in beginning to worry. If we are to give complete sovereignty to the people of West Germany, who are we thereafter to tell them that they may not relieve the sufferings of their brothers in the eastern zone of Germany? I should like to underline what the Leader of the Opposition said when he said that the paramount interest of the people of West Germany is the reunification of Germany.
I was one of those lucky enough to hear the former prime minister of Great Britain, Right Hon. Clement Attlee, speaking in Vancouver on Saturday last. He said that the question of what our foreign policy is depends to the greatest extent on where you are.
Now, I ask this house, where are we in Canada? I follow that with another question and I think it is a logical one. It is this. Can Canada be defended? I doubt that very much; I doubt whether Canada can be defended. About a week before Easter the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) was unable or unwilling to assure the Canadian people that we have even as much as one atom bomb in Canada. He was unwilling to give his citizens that assurance.
In connection with the matter of research, to which the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) so ably referred this afternoon, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) had been smart I think he would have assured the Canadian people that he would appoint the top scientists of the dominion to make sure that these thermonuclear weapons will not have-

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit an observation? If he looks at the statement I made in this house on April 4, he will find I did that very thing.

I am glad to know the minister has announced that a committee of the top scientists of Canada has been appointed to investigate the possible effect on the Canadian people. This was new to me, and I thank the minister for that interjection. I hope I have not misinterpreted what he said.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the people of India, southeast Asia, Great Britain, western Europe and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, considering where they are in the world, must have world peace. Each of these nations, if a major war should break out- let us not play with the idea of minor wars-both right and wrong, will go down to defeat in the holocaust that will ensue.
I hope that nothing I say is going to label me as an opponent of the veterans of Canada. If there are people in Canada who think other than as I do, and if they are willing to make the supreme sacrifice and I am one of the fortunate ones to survive a war, then my first responsibility is to see that these people are as adequately cared for as the rich resources of our nation will make possible.
Also, I shall have no truck with the so-called peace front in Canada. I do not believe in any so-called righteous war against the so-called capitalist oppressors. I do not believe any war or any revolution has ever resolved anything in human history. I come back again to the fact that, if absolute values exist in the world, then absolute values will continue to exist, wars notwithstanding. There are vested interests on both sides. There is the vested interest of imperialist communism and there is the vested interest of international capitalism. I say, a plague on both your houses. We want peace and prosperity in the world for all the people of the world.

speechtext:
I was
not going to say anything in this debate, but I should like to correct something that I do not think is altogether fair in the statement made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. First, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Du-fresne) on the speech that he made. I have not always agreed with him, but I do not believe he ever spoke more sincerely than he did today. He came right to the point expressed so ably by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that love is stronger than hate and faith is stronger than doubt.
I agreed with the hon. member who has just taken his seat when he said he was 
proud of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) when he made his statements away from home. He was proud to be a Canadian and so was I. But I think he just slipped a little bit when he said that these statements were spoiled when the minister came home and met the Liberal association. I do not believe the minister ever met the Liberal association before he made his statement. The implication is that the minister is one thing at home and another thing away. As I know the minister, he has always given of his best, whether he was on third base on the baseball diamond, in his home, in this house or in Europe. I stand behind the minister 100 per cent in all his statements. He has stood for peace, and peace with honour.
I was talking to an official who served with the army in Korea. He told me two things that I think this house should know. First, he said that communism was failing in China. He proved this by saying the communists were trying to break up the home life in China. Home life has been sacred to the people of China for hundreds and thousands of years, and they do not like it. He proved his statement by saying that refugees are arriving by thousands in Hong Kong. I do not remember the exact number of people who have come into Hong Kong, but I believe the population has increased by over 2 million. These people would not serve under communist rule. The streets are lined with people sleeping side by side on little mats. He said there is a feeling over there that there is going to be a revolution before too long; that may or may not be true.
Another thing this captain told me, and I was thinking about it when the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) was speaking about Korea, was that Korea is hopeful. He said that there was a church a day built and organized in Korea every day for the last three years. I think that is outstanding, and it proves the statement made by the hon. member for Quebec West, that these people appreciate the kindness of the members of the church and that love will win out.
Another reason why I am speaking tonight is the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). I cannot quote his exact words because my memory would not allow that, but he said the young men of the country should be organized for military training for four or five months of the year, say from November 1 to April 1. He has shown wisdom in that statement, even though he comes from the west. I feel this would be splendid training for the young men who may be out of work,

and would it not be a splendid remedy for those who are out of work for a few months each year? Again I congratulate the minister upon sticking to his guns in the fight for peace with honour.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to close this debate I would be ungrateful indeed if in the first place I did not express my appreciation of the encouragement and support I have just received from the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and tell him in reply that I shall be very glad to play third base for him any place, any time.
Mr. Speaker, this debate began on March 24 and, with appropriate intermissions, is finishing on April 21. During the days that have been allotted to the discussion of this subject-and there are few subjects which will come before us which will be more important-the discussion has ranged far and wide, from the atomic pollution of the atmosphere, on which my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) speaks with such enviable assurance, to the Old Testament, its history and its mores, about which the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Mac-Dougall) talked to us some days ago.
To a very large extent, however, the discussion has been focused on the situation in the Far East, though other subjects have been brought up, and a great many questions have been asked. Tonight I hope to deal with some of those questions. Also I feel I must challenge one or two observations made during the course of the debate which I do not think were correct. It may be that I shall not be able to deal adequately with all the matters raised, in which case I ask the pardon of those whom I have overlooked.
When the committee on external affairs has the estimates before it-and that is the purpose of our present resolution-of course there will be opportunity before that committee to question the minister on any matter raised in this debate, or any other matter concerning the policy or the administration of the Department of External Affairs. As is customary, I shall be very glad to make myself available to that committee for as long as it desires to question me.
In this debate more than one speaker has referred to the valuable part being played in these tense and difficult times by the association to which we belong, and of which we are very proud, our commonwealth of nations. I believe we are all conscious, probably now as much as ever before in our
External Affairs
history, of the value of that association- especially in the service it is now performing not only for the nations of the commonwealth, but for the world at large in providing a bridge, one of the few effective bridges, between the free East and the free West.
In his contribution to the debate the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) devoted most of his speech to our commonwealth of nations. He advocated-and in certain sections of the house this has been advocated for years-what he called the strengthening of our commonwealth. Among other things he asked what was the basic difference between the commonwealth and, let us say, the United Nations. He asked what was the difference between our relationship with members of the commonwealth and with, let us say, a country like Brazil.
Well, if he had attended meetings of the United Nations assembly or other United Nations agencies-and I hope he will have that opportunity-and if he had attended commonwealth discussions, I think he would sense . at once the difference between the two associations. And that is not of course to depreciate the value of the association of the United Nations.
The basic difference in the commonwealth relationship is that it has been formed, has grown up and has been built on the habit and the tradition of co-operation. We have developed within the commonwealth a feeling of close unity. There is a genuine understanding among its members to work together in peace and in war, and a strong desire to co-operate and to work out agreed policies and agreed solutions to problems, even when it is not always possible to do so. And then of course we have the great advantage of a common head in the commonwealth, both for the monarchical and the republican members, and also the bond of common parliamentary institutions and parliamentary traditions.
The hon. member for Oxford feels that we should strengthen these bonds, and that we should develop what he has called a central secretariat. He says that we should also try to work out an intra-commonwealth defence force. Well I would suggest to the hon. member-and this is a matter which has been discussed often both in and out of the house-that if the members of the commonwealth tried to build up some strong and centralized machinery, if they tried to build up a centralized intra-commonwealth defence force, far from strengthening this association it might, indeed, weaken it to the point where it would disappear, at least in the sense in which it exists today.

External Affairs
I think the commonwealth in its present form and organization is doing a most valuable and important service. One of the most useful things about the commonwealth is that it does include within its membership a variety of peoples, at times antagonistic peoples; and if we tried to bring those peoples together in any formal and organized way, for defence or by exclusive economic cooperation, far from strengthening the association we might indeed weaken it.
The hon. member to whom I have referred, while he did not underestimate the difficulties, rather expressed the hope that by this kind of development-and I think I am quoting him correctly-the commonwealth might become or lead to a third power bloc which would be powerful enough to act as a counterbalance to the United States and Russia.
With all respect, Mr. Speaker, I submit that this third force concept, whether it is a commonwealth concept or any other group of states, is a dangerous one, because it would mean that, in a sense, we in the commonwealth were separating ourselves from the United States and coming between the United States and the NATO powers on the one hand and Soviet imperialist communist powers on the other.
I think it is much better to stick to the concept of two blocs, two forces in the world -if there have to be two-the forces of peace and the forces that we think threaten the peace. It is better to line ourselves up with the former and welcome into its ranks any free states wishing to join it. One specific respect in which the commonwealth has been playing a useful part in recent years-and this is a matter which has been referred to by a good many speakers-is in the provision of technical and capital assistance to underdeveloped countries, especially those in southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent under what we call the Colombo plan. The Colombo plan, of course, is more than a commonwealth arrangement; but it was commonwealth in inspiration and organization. It has proved its value and I hope it will continue to do so.
In this debate, some very strong criticism has been levelled at the government by my hon. friends opposite and by some members of the official opposition, that we have not played an honourable part in this Colombo plan; that what we have done was-I think the words were-a mere pittance, or, as it was referred to by one speaker, an insult to the needs of the problem. Well, of course, Mr. Speaker, as is nearly always the case in any human endeavour, we could have done more. But to keep this project in perspective I need only point out that in the four years of the plan, capital and technical assistance
[Mr. Pearson.1
from outside the countries which are members of the plan has been contributed to the amount of $1,300,000,000; last year $340 million, of which Canada will have contributed $128,400,000. That is not large in terms of expenditure on other things. I would be the first to admit that; but I would point out to those who criticize us so bitterly-perhaps "bitterly" is not a fair word, but criticize us so strongly-and I am not objecting to that-and who relate our expenditures in this field to those which we have to make on defence, that the primacy of expenditures on defence is admitted by those very countries which we are helping and who need our help; it is admitted to a point where some of these countries which are receiving capital assistance-and I say this in no way of criticism at all-are now devoting more than half of their already inadequate budget to defence. And some of those countries that are devoting such a high percentage of their budget to defence are the first to proclaim that they have no feeling of menace from attack by outside communist states. I mention this merely to try to show that this is not as simple a problem as is sometimes portrayed. Also, while not unduly satisfied or smug, or certainly not boasting about what we have done, I am not going to be apologetic about it.
I would prefer in this regard to quote the verdict of an outside source, the Economist, a magazine which is often quoted in this house and which, writing about the Colombo plan progress report on December 25, 1954, had this to say:
On the contributing side of the plan, the part played by Australia and Canada is particularly striking.
The Economist went on to say:
In spite of the undoubted achievements of the plan in the past three years, it will be necessary not only to maintain the momentum of economic development in the area but to increase it.
I agree with that. I continue:
But it is not simply a question of finance. Expert technical advice and training is of equal importance, and in this direction the technical co-operation scheme, together with other parallel projects of technical assistance, has undoubtedly played a major part. It is equally important to get more effective planning as well as better management and administration. None of these tasks can be solved quickly. The Colombo plan's future tasks are measured not in years but in decades.
And so, Mr. Speaker, while none of us needs to be satisfied with what we have done, I think we can look forward to a continuation of this plan with resources from this and other countries and with an even greater field for usefulness than it has had in the past.

A planning conference has been set for Singapore next September, when the whole future of the plan is to be examined, particularly in its relationship to United States support, which has been, if I may say so, somewhat more forthcoming in recent months than previously.
The discussion of the Colombo plan brings me to the main subject which has occupied most of our attention in this debate and which I dealt with when I introduced the resolution some time ago, namely international developments in the Far East. Discussion of that subject has, to a very large extent in this debate, revolved around our Canadian relationship with the United States, to a point where it has been difficult at times to disentangle the two things. I think it is a normal and healthy sign that we should be so preoccupied in this house in a debate on external affairs with the most important aspect of our foreign relations at the present time, namely our relationship with the United States of America. I think of that relationship, important as it is bilaterally to us, in terms of collective action, in terms of collective defence, not merely as something between Canada and the United States, but as something between Canada, the United States and its friends in NATO and in the United Nations. I also try to distinguish, in this defence relationship with the United States, the problems which may come from what we have begun to call peripheral conflicts from those which will be posed by a major all-out war of extermination.
Hon. members will recall that when I spoke some time ago in this debate I tried to make this distinction clear. So far as these peripheral wars, those smaller wars, if you wish to call them that, are concerned, Canada, both through its relationship to the United States and through its relationship to the United Nations or to NATO, might be involved in them. But Canada can hardly remain aloof from the latter. We are also concerned with those smaller conflicts because of the danger that they may spread into a larger conflict. There is no better example of that danger than the situation in and around Formosa and the coastal islands. It is possible, of course, that even if trouble were at the beginning limited to that area, it might spread to this continent. If it did spread to this continent it would be very difficult for us to remain aloof from its effect. The facts of geography, apart from other things, would indicate that. Well, how can it spread? It might spread not by any all-out massive attack from some Chinese communist government on the North American continent, because that would not be
External Affairs
possible under present conditions. It might spread by a reaction on the part of the Chinese government's allies, a reaction on the part of the Soviet union, which would result in a massive all-out attack on this continent, the Soviet union being the only power today on the other side which is capable of that kind of reaction.
Now, if that reaction took place as a result of a local conflict in China, that would be an aggression; it would be a violation of the United Nations charter and we would be asked to undertake the commitments which we have accepted as members of the United Nations or the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
When speaking on this aspect of the question some days ago, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that if war broke out over Formosa or over the coastal islands that kind of chain reaction would be absolutely inevitable. I think I ought to quote him at this point because this seems to me to be of importance. Referring to the Secretary of State for External Affairs he said, as reported on page 2350 of Hansard of March 24:
He has but to read the words of Molotov in which he stated that the situation in Asia was of equal concern to the U.S.S.R. In that case it is but fantasy to say that what might happen over there would not become an all-embracing conflict.
I did not go as far as that and indeed I do not think the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) went quite as far as that in his statement, but I do admit that that kind of conflict might spread even though it was not inevitable that it would. I feel, and I am sure that hon. members on all sides of the house must feel, that if it did spread, if that did happen and there was a massive aggressive air attack on this continent, a struggle in which the very existence of the people of the United States and of Canada would be at stake, all our continental, all our NATO defence arrangements and our whole system of collective security which we have built up over recent years would come into play. In that kind of situation, and I limit it to that kind of situation, how could we be neutral?
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) himself admitted this in his statement. I should like to quote from what he said, as reported on page 2877 of Hansard of April 6:
Now, if the minister were merely saying that if a world-wide conflagration breaks out, particularly bearing in mind the power blocs that exist in the world today, because of our geographical position, to put it in the vernacular, we would have had it, one could hardly argue with him.

External Affairs
His leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), had this to say, as reported on page 2356 of Hansard:
Perhaps the minister is right. Perhaps if they- Referring to the United States of America. -were engaged in a major war it would involve us automatically, because of our geographical position with them.
I think that in the circumstances which I have mentioned that is self-evident, but I do not from that draw any such deduction as has been drawn by certain members of this house, most noticeably this afternoon, the most irresponsible being that by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer); I do not draw any deduction from that statement of automatic assurance of support or willingness to intervene on behalf of or with the United States in any war, major or minor, on the continent of China or any place else where that kind of intervention would take place. Whether support in those circumstances could be counted on from Canada would depend entirely on whether our commitments under NATO were involved, whether there was aggression under the United Nations charter.
I want to be quite clear about that. Anything that I said in Toronto and anything that I have said here-I hoped I had made this quite clear the other day but apparently it was not clear enough for the hon. member for Three Rivers-does not mean nor could it fairly be interpreted as meaning that whenever the United States is at war we are bound to participate. It does not mean that we have any obligation to participate in any war except a war against aggression within the principles of the United Nations charter.
Now when I say that, and I am merely repeating what I said in the house the other day, the hon. member for Prince Albert complains that this-I use his own expression- is watering down our support for United States policy which I gave in my Toronto speech. I do not think it is watering down anything at all. What I tried to do the other day, and what I am trying again to do tonight, is to squeeze some water out of the interpretation given to that Toronto speech by careless commentators. Nevertheless, whatever I may have done in the way of squeezing water out, the speech still seems to remain too strong for my friends of the C.C.F. party.
The position that they take, if I interpret that position correctly, is that while this statement in the circumstances which I have mentioned may be true, I should not have said it because it might be misconstrued in the United States and because of that misconstruction they will feel, as someone put it, that they now have Canada in the bag, that 
our influence will have been weakened or will even possibly have vanished in Washington.
Who would be fooling whom by remaining silent about Canada's position in the conditions which I have outlined? We certainly would not be fooling the United States government by our silence, because they know of our relationship to them in NATO and they know of the relationship which we have built up with them under NATO in respect of continental defence. I hope that silence in this matter would not be fooling any potential enemy, because if it did that it would be bad.
However, it might possibly fool our own people. Silence might be misinterpreted in this country with unhappy results for which the government would rightly be criticized. I prefer the verdict in this matter of the Daily Telegraph in London to that of my hon. friends opposite. The Daily Telegraph, referring to Canada and the United States, had this to say in an editorial:
The conclusion to be drawn from the interdependence of the two nations in a major war is not, as some of Mr. Pearson's critics have suggested, that the United States can take Canadian support in a circumstance for granted, and therefore may disregard Canadian views. On the contrary, it gives the Canadian government both the right and the duty to warn and to dissuade.
That remains our right and I hope that we will exercise it on appropriate occasions in Washington. It is also our duty and I hope that we will discharge it on appropriate occasions. It seems to me that the moral of this position is that if all these dangers surround us, little wars with their obligations, or big wars with all their catastrophes, if we are surrounded by these dangers, then the moral is to do everything we possibly can to stop any war before it starts.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is not in his seat tonight, but I know he has good reason for not being here. I would prefer to refer to his speech in his presence, but I should like to quote what he said, as reported on page 2356 of Hansard:
But I wish to suggest this, that the Canadian people want our government to state forthrightly and without equivocation that we will do everything we possibly can do to ensure that Canada's influence and Canada's policy, especially in its relations with the United States, will be directed toward the avoidance of conflict, political and economic.
We have already given that assurance, but if it will make my hon. friends feel any better I am quite happy to repeat unequivocally that assurance tonight in this house. If we fail, and we might fail, then I suggest that our policy be this: when possible, to

limit conflicts, to prevent them spreading, and then to end them. There is no other policy in the mind of any member of this government.
This debate, Mr. Speaker, has done something else which has caused a good many of us-I know that it has caused me-some anxiety. In certain sections of the house- and I am referring now to the members of the C.C.F. party-it has underlined a very deep uneasiness which they in particular feel about United States policy. That anxiety-and "anxiety" is certainly not too strong a word in view of some of the expressions that have been used in this debate-was expressed both by the leader of the C.C.F. party and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In my view these hon. members, for whom, as they know, I have great respect, and others in their group who spoke, presented an unfair and unbalanced picture of the situation, especially in respect of the United States' attitudes and policy towards Asia. I am now talking about the situation in the Far East. I was especially disappointed, and indeed distressed, by the analysis which was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, not so much of the policy, but of the purpose of the policy of the secretary of state of the United States. On page 2878 of Hansard he said this:
I think it is Mr. Dulles' primary purpose to keep war away from the United States.
A few words later, he says:
If he can keep war away from the United States-if he can keep it in the Pescadores, in Quemoy, in Matsu or in northern Canada-his aim is met. His aim is to keep war away from continental United States.
We may have differences of opinion with Mr. Dulles on matters of policy. I have had them myself, and no doubt will continue to have them. We may have one view or the other about the wisdom of his policy, but I think that it is most unfair to suggest that the secretary of state of the United States, who is serving in the government of President Eisenhower, has any other purpose than that which we have in this house, to keep war away and not merely away from the continental United States. I would not like that kind of statement to go on the record of this house without the kind of challenge that I am giving it now.
The hon. member also said-and this sentiment was echoed by other members of his group-that our foreign policy should be made in Ottawa only and not in Washington. Well, Mr. Speaker, as long as Canada is a sovereign state, the decisions in foreign policy and any other policies have to be made in this parliament of Canada. That is a very
External Affairs
different thing from saying that our policy can only be made in Ottawa and should not be made or even influenced anywhere else. Foreign policy in this world of interdependence cannot be made in any one country or any one capital no matter how powerful that country or capital may be. We are working together today in a peace coalition, and the very essence of that coalition is that every member of it acts only after discussion and consultation with others. In that sense each member must influence the other members' policy, and I hope it will remain that way, because that is the way it should be. That gives our best chance for peace, by collective policy and collective action. In this respect I am distinguishing between decision and the formulation of policy. Suppose the United States adopted that maxim and made its own policy solely in Washington, or the United Kingdom decided to make its policy solely in London, or the French government solely in Paris; it would not be long before the North Atlantic Treaty Organization would itself dissolve. If it dissolved we would not be worrying so much about whether we were making our own policy; we would be worrying far more about our protection against potential enemies even than we do now.
Foreign policy in a coalition working for peace is bound to operate collectively if it is to succeed. That does not mean that we are merely tagging along behind American decisions. It may be that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre and some of his colleagues think so. He himself said, as reported on page 2877 of Hansard:
We feel the result is that Canada has said-
This refers to my statement in Toronto.
-that we regard ourselves as quite free to make any decisions we want with regard to foreign policy, so long as they are agreed to by Washington.
Well, Mr. Speaker, with all respect, that is a distorted and unfair interpretation of what I said in Toronto or what I have said in this house, and I only need mention one example to prove how unfair it is. Has Washington agreed to our statement of policy that we will not intervene in Matsu or Quemoy if they are attacked by the forces of communist China? We have made that statement and I am happy to repeat it tonight, but it was not made, nor was the policy decided, after any agreement in Washington; on the contrary. That statement then was unfounded.
Another statement from the same group was made to the effect that apparently I feel now that I have to go along very easily and readily with the views of the secretary of state of the United States. I hope that Mr. Dulles' views will be such that I can go along with them easily and readily, but I can assure

External Affairs
you, sir, if any assurance is needed, that I will not hesitate to disagree with them when I feel that it is undesirable and unwise to support them. It seems to me that the trouble with my hon. friends in the C.C.F. party in these matters is that they take a jaundiced and morbidly suspicious view of everything that goes on in the United States, or at least in the United States official circles. As was pointed out this afternoon in what I thought was a very effective intervention by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott), sometimes they mistake the clamour and confusion of voices in that vigorous, free democracy for the authentic expression of United States policy. I suggest, therefore, that occasionally they look a little more closely behind the headlines. I also suggest with respect that they look across-not across the border so often-but across the ocean to some of the real sources of danger to peace in the world today from communist imperialism.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and others have done just that. They have looked across the Pacific, and they have found many things which they did not like. I think we can all share to some extent their feeling of uneasiness. But I myself thought-and I hope I am not being unfair to him in saying it-that the statement of the leader of the C.C.F. party on this matter was not a fair presentation of the case. He attacked very vigorously indeed the Chinese government on Formosa and its leader Chiang Kai-shek and what he called his "bloodthirsty war lords". He did not see fit in this statement of his to make any such attack on the Chinese communist government in Peking. He emphasized the danger to peace from Chiang. But I want to point out-as has been pointed out by others, particularly I think by my friend the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Fraser)-that it is not Chiang Kai-shek that we are concerned with on Formosa. It is peace and the defence of a people against communist aggression.
He also-and I take particular exception to this, Mr. Speaker-talked about not only danger from Chiang Kai-shek but danger from the United States. This is at page 2357 of Hansard. He emphasized the danger of being dragged into a war by the policies that are now being pursued by the secretary of state of the United States. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we are in much more danger of being dragged into war by policies that are pursued by the foreign minister in Peking and by the foreign minister in Moscow than we are by the policies pursued by the secretary of state of the United States.
No one wishes to adopt a provocative or bellicose attitude toward any government,

communist or otherwise. We are obliged to coexist with them in this world, whether we like it or not. But when the leader of a party in a debate of this kind will spend so much time attacking the policies of our friends, I think he might have spared a word or two for the dangers which might come to peace from the policies of those whom we have some reason to fear.
In his statement he outlined what his own policy-and I presume he was speaking for his group-towards China in the present situation would be. I have just jotted down the four points he made on that occasion. The first was that we should exile Chiang Kai-shek-and this suggestion has been repeated by other members of his party-presumably by force. 1 do not know who is anxious to take part in that particular expedition.
I have no brief for the government of Chiang Kai-shek. I am not going to object to the facts which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) stated about the atrocities that were committed in Formosa in 1947, just about ten years ago. It was a dark page in the history of that island and in the history of China. But I would ask him to go a little bit beyond 1947 and to read reports which have been appearing in the Manchester Guardian recently by their correspondent, a wise and unprejudiced observer, as to the improvement that has taken place in the government of Formosa in recent years. We do not in this government have to subscribe to the policies of Chiang Kai-shek; we also have a fairly open mind about the future of Formosa and indeed we have been criticized because we have not been more specific in our policy in this regard. But I certainly do not subscribe to any policy which would ask us to share in the ejection of Chiang Kai-shek and half a million Chinese nationalist soldiers from Formosa.
The second suggestion the leader of the C.C.F. made was that we should neutralize Formosa and place it under a trusteeship. I think there is a good deal to be said for that suggestion. That may prove to be the wisest solution to this extremely difficult problem. I think, however, it is premature to be dogmatic on the point or to make up our minds finally on anything like that at the present time. A great deal of discussion is now going on in diplomatic channels as to how this problem of Formosa can be solved in a way which will meet the wishes of the Formosan people and will take that island out of conflict. The solution may turn out to be the neutralization of Formosa and a trusteeship under the United Nations. That may turn out to be the wisest solution. But

I would point out that that particular solution, namely to put Formosa under United Nations trusteeship, is about the only single thing on which the Chinese communists and the Chinese national government agree. They are both violently opposed to it.
So far as Canadian responsibility is concerned over Formosa-I think this had better be repeated, and I will try to make it clear- we have no other commitment in regard to Formosa than that which arises from our membership in the United Nations. That was the position a year ago and that is the position today. We feel that the status of Formosa has not yet been finally determined but we also feel that the communist government in Peking should not use force to bring about that determination. This afternoon my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre-

speechtext: -or rather the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) had something to say about a press report of a statement made or alleged to have been made in Australia by my friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). speechtext: Have you not cabled him already?
